World.title: US gross national debt passes 40 trillion dollars for the first time
World.content:
US gross national debt passes 40 trillion dollars for the first time

20th Thursday, August 2026 - 08:20 UTC Full article

The increase is not the work of a single administration. It grew sharply under Joe Biden, with the spending programmes deployed during the pandemic, and has accelerated since Donald Trump's return

The gross public debt of the United States reached 40.047 trillion dollars on Tuesday, according to data released by the Treasury Department. It is the first time the figure has crossed that threshold, and it has arrived earlier than expected: the Congressional Budget Office had projected 39.4 trillion by the end of fiscal 2026 and placed the jump to 40 trillion in 2027.

Of that total, 32.266 trillion is debt held by the public — private investors, funds and foreign holders — and 7.782 trillion is intragovernmental debt, meaning securities the federal government owes to its own trust funds, among them social security. Gross debt is equivalent to 124% of gross domestic product, the highest level since the Second World War.

The figure comes at a time of rising borrowing costs. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond climbed to 5.3%, its highest since 2007, forcing the government to refinance at the steepest rates since before the 2008 financial crisis. Markets attribute the rise to doubts over the path of inflation and the deficit, to spending linked to the war with Iran, and to borrowing by large technology companies to fund artificial intelligence investment.

The deficit for the fiscal year ending on September 30 is projected at 2.1 trillion dollars, close to 6% of GDP. July's monthly shortfall reached 432.3 billion, the largest in more than five years. The cost of servicing the debt will rise to 1.4 trillion this year and is expected within two years to exceed social security as the largest single item of government spending.

“The gross national debt has doubled in the last ten years; in less than twenty years, it has quadrupled,” said Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan organisation. A decade ago the figure stood at 19.4 trillion.

The increase is not the work of a single administration. It grew sharply under Joe Biden, with the spending programmes deployed during the pandemic, and has accelerated since Donald Trump's return, driven by military spending, refunds of tariffs struck down in the courts and the tax cuts included in the budget law passed at the start of his second term. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this month that the administration inherited “a mess” from its predecessor, and announced he would double debt buybacks in secondary markets to bring down financing costs.

The Congressional Budget Office warned earlier this year that the fiscal trajectory “is not sustainable” and projected that debt held by the public will rise from 101% of GDP this year to 120% in 2036, surpassing the record 106% recorded in 1946.

World.title: A judge demands urgent reports from Argentina's government on the fate of road funds
World.content:
A judge demands urgent reports from Argentina's government on the fate of road funds

20th Thursday, August 2026 - 08:13 UTC Full article

Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier on Tuesday denied at the Casa Rosada that any misuse of funds had occurred

Federal judge Ernesto Kreplak, sitting in La Plata, this week admitted a class action and requested urgent reports from the Ministry of Economy, the National Roads Directorate and Banco Nación on the use of resources from the Integrated Road System (SisVial), a trust fund financed by the tax on liquid fuels whose legal purpose is the construction and maintenance of national highways.

The case originated in an investigation by the newspaper La Nación, according to which 1,503,252 million pesos entered the fund between January 2024 and May 2026, of which 394,406 million were spent on road works, or 26.2% of the total. As of May 31, the fund held more than one trillion pesos — around 670 million dollars — in government bonds and fixed-term deposits. Execution stood at 11.3% in 2024, 39% in 2025 and 18.5% in the first five months of this year.

Some 28.58% of fuel tax revenue goes to the Transport Infrastructure Trust, and half of that share corresponds to SisVial.

Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier on Tuesday denied at the Casa Rosada that any misuse of funds had occurred. Days earlier he had told provincial media that part of the revenue had gone “towards achieving fiscal balance,” one of the pillars of Javier Milei's economic policy. Ravier said the government's new approach is for national highways to be financed by private investment rather than tax revenue. Of the 40,000 kilometres of national road network, the executive has tendered 9,000.

The class action was brought by lawmaker Victoria Tolosa Paz, who also filed a criminal complaint. “The government charges a fuel tax to maintain our roads and, instead of spending it on works, three out of every four pesos from SisVial went into financial gambling,” she said. A separate complaint by lawmaker Marcela Pagano was assigned to judge Julio Ercolini, who as of this week had not referred it to a prosecutor. No officials have been charged and no criminal case has been formally opened.

Subsequent reporting extended the pattern to other funds. According to the fact-checking outlet Chequeado, of the 375,000 million pesos collected since early 2024 for water works, around a third was executed, with the remainder placed in Treasury bills and deposits.

The national roads workers' union says 70% of highways are in fair to poor condition. Milei announced in 2024 the elimination of trust funds, which he called “political slush funds”; around 27 remain active, with their administration concentrated in the Ministry of Economy.

World.title: Harry and Meghan will move to the UK without resuming official royal duties
World.content:
Harry and Meghan will move to the UK without resuming official royal duties

20th Thursday, August 2026 - 08:06 UTC Full article

According to the same sources, Meghan will continue running her As Ever company from the United Kingdom

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, will settle in the United Kingdom from this autumn, though they will not resume their roles as working members of the royal family, British media reported on Wednesday. The story was broken by The Telegraph and corroborated to the Associated Press by a person close to the couple who was not authorised to speak publicly. There has been no official statement from the palace or the Sussexes.

Their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, are already enrolled at British schools and will start classes in September. The family will live at a private, non-royal residence outside London, while keeping their home in Montecito, California, and a holiday property in Portugal.

According to the same sources, Meghan will continue running her As Ever company from the United Kingdom, while Harry, the younger son of King Charles III, will be able to devote more time to the British charities he works with.

The move comes six years after the couple gave up their official duties, in March 2020, and settled in California. Their departure, dubbed “Megxit” by the British press, followed a meeting convened by Queen Elizabeth II at her Sandringham residence, which concluded that a partial role within the royal household was not workable.

From the United States, the couple maintained a public confrontation with the monarchy. In a 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey they said a member of the royal family, whom they did not name, had made a comment about Archie's future skin tone before he was born. Elizabeth II responded with a statement saying the issues raised would be addressed privately and that recollections of events “may vary.” Meghan also said the Princess of Wales had made her cry before their 2018 wedding. That same year, allegations that she had bullied palace staff were published, which she denied.

In 2021 the Queen stripped her grandson of his military titles and royal patronages. The criticism continued in a Netflix documentary and in the duke's autobiography, Spare, published after Elizabeth II's death, in which he described a physical altercation with his brother William and called Queen Camilla “dangerous.” The palaces did not comment on those passages.

A YouGov survey in July put favourable views of Meghan at 22%, against 65% unfavourable; for Harry the figures were 33% and 58%. In 2024, after Charles III was diagnosed with cancer, the duke travelled to London to see him and the two spent less than 45 minutes together.

World.title: A critical report says Argentina's investment regime concentrated capital in mining and oil
World.content:
A critical report says Argentina's investment regime concentrated capital in mining and oil

19th Wednesday, August 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

In February, a decree brought hydrocarbon exploration and production projects into the regime, extended the application deadline to July 2027 and eased conditions for expanding admitted projects

Argentina's Large Investment Incentive Regime (RIGI), created in 2024, “consolidated a strongly extractive profile and did not stimulate new sectors,” according to a report released on Wednesday by the RIGI Observatory, a coalition of civil society organisations and academic centres that examines the scheme from a critical standpoint.

The regime grants thirty years of tax, customs and foreign exchange benefits to companies investing more than 200 million dollars in sectors deemed strategic. According to official data cited in the report, 44 projects have applied to join, worth 198,979 million dollars, of which 21 have been admitted for a total of 46,708 million. Among those approved, twelve are in mining, five in oil and gas and the remaining four in energy, infrastructure and steel. Of the 23 projects under evaluation, thirteen are in hydrocarbons and seven in mining. Other records consulted show lower figures for earlier periods.

The document says investment is concentrated in oil, copper, gas and lithium, while activities listed among the regime's stated objectives — tourism, forestry industry and renewable energy — show marginal participation or no projects at all. It also notes that fewer than half the initiatives involve foreign capital.

In February, a decree brought hydrocarbon exploration and production projects into the regime, extended the application deadline to July 2027 and eased conditions for expanding projects already admitted. According to the report, this extended an exceptional scheme to the Vaca Muerta formation, which already recorded record levels of investment, production and exports and had earlier promotion policies in place. Filings rose after the decree, mostly linked to that basin.

The text also argues the period coincided with a rollback in environmental regulation, citing a reform of the Glaciers Law that the authors say permits mining activity near ice fields.

On fiscal cost, the Centre for Argentine Political Economy estimated it at around 1,069 million dollars a year once approved projects reach full operation, between 2029 and 2033. In response to a freedom of information request, the government said the first twelve admitted projects foresee disbursements of 1,920 million dollars over their first two years.

The executive is pushing through Congress a new scheme, informally called the “super RIGI,” aimed at activities with no prior development in the country, among them data centres and artificial intelligence, with a floor of 1 billion dollars. It provides for a 15% income tax rate, accelerated depreciation and the removal of export duties from the outset. The Observatory argues it would not correct the imbalances of the current scheme.

World.title: A personalized mRNA therapy passes a phase 3 melanoma trial for the first time
World.content:
A personalized mRNA therapy passes a phase 3 melanoma trial for the first time

19th Wednesday, August 2026 - 21:47 UTC Full article

Despite the vaccine label used in much of the coverage, this is not a preventive measure but a treatment

Pharmaceutical companies Merck, known as MSD outside the United States and Canada, and Moderna announced on Wednesday that their individualized neoantigen therapy, intismeran autogene, met its endpoints in a phase 3 trial in melanoma patients. It is the first positive result at that stage for an mRNA-based cancer treatment.

The INTerpath-001 study enrolled 1,137 patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV melanoma and no prior systemic treatment. Participants were assigned in a two-to-one ratio: one group received intismeran combined with pembrolizumab, the immunotherapy Merck markets as Keytruda, and the other pembrolizumab alone, the standard of care in that setting. The trial met its primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival and its secondary endpoint of distant metastasis-free survival.

Despite the vaccine label used in much of the coverage, this is not a preventive measure but a treatment. Each patient's resected tumour is analysed to identify the mutations specific to that cancer, and that information is used to design a tailored mRNA therapy intended to train the immune system to recognise and attack malignant cells should they return.

The companies did not disclose the size of the benefit observed. Their statement describes “statistically significant and clinically meaningful” improvements over pembrolizumab alone, without figures. Full data will be presented at an international medical meeting, and both companies will begin talks with regulators on filing for approval.

In the earlier phase 2 trial, with 157 patients, five-year data presented this year at the American Society of Clinical Oncology meeting showed a 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death and a 59% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis or death.

Marisol Soengas, head of the melanoma group at Spain's National Cancer Research Centre, said researchers would have preferred to see the data. “Given the track record and standing of the companies, cautiously, there is reason for optimism,” she said. She warned about the cost of the technology and how it would fit into public health systems. Luis Álvarez-Vallina, of the same centre, cautioned when the phase 2 results were presented that melanoma is a particularly immunogenic tumour, so the findings may not extrapolate to other cancers.

Moderna shares rose more than 90% in early New York trading, to around 120 dollars, while Merck's gained between 7% and 12%, according to different agencies. The joint clinical programme comprises nine phase 2 and phase 3 trials in melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancer.

World.title: Falklands consolidates the future of its economy in the fishing and hydrocarbons industries
World.content:
Falklands consolidates the future of its economy in the fishing and hydrocarbons industries

19th Wednesday, August 2026 - 10:01 UTC Full article

In late 2025 Fortuna Ltd acquired Ocean Fish Group, a fishing and processing company based in Cornwall, England.

The Falklands Planning and Building Committee has approved two projects tied to the sectors that underpin the Islands' economy: fishing and hydrocarbons.

A local construction company submitted plans seeking permission to erect 160 modular housing units, in a two-storey complex with capacity for 320 beds, intended to accommodate personnel working on the development of the offshore Sea Lion field, operated by Israel's Navitas Petroleum alongside Britain's Rockhopper Exploration, which holds 35% of the licenses. Hydrocarbon extraction is anticipated to begin during the first half of 2028.

The plans indicate the complex will include parking and ample space for the storage of equipment and materials. The site is the same one used in 2013 to set up a demountable hotel alongside a works compound for a similar purpose, an effort abandoned at the time because of oil price volatility.

The site sits far enough from the center of the capital, Stanley, to avoid noise pollution, and has sufficient roadway to safeguard pedestrians. Following those clarifications, consultations with neighbors and the oil company's commitment to meet the conditions, the plans were approved, the Committee indicated.

At the same sitting, the Committee approved plans from Fortuna Ltd, the Islands' largest fishing company, which sought authorization to build new offices commensurate with the volume of business it has consolidated. Stanley-based Fortuna is the Falklands' largest quota and license holder for Loligo and Illex squid, finfish and Patagonian toothfish. In November 2025 it acquired Ocean Fish Group, a fishing and processing business in Cornwall, England, having bought tug operator Holyhead Towing in Anglesey, Wales, the previous year.

World.title: An Argentine consultant who advised Milei's campaign detained in Bolivia after a shooting
World.content:
An Argentine consultant who advised Milei's campaign detained in Bolivia after a shooting

19th Wednesday, August 2026 - 09:52 UTC Full article

The 33-year-old lawyer underwent surgery and survived; none of the rounds struck vital organs. The case is being investigated as attempted femicide

Bolivian police detained Argentine political consultant Fernando Cerimedo in the early hours of Tuesday at Viru Viru international airport in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, hours after his former partner, Bolivian lawyer Nadia Beller, was shot three times outside a hotel in the city. Cerimedo has not been formally charged and his involvement in the attack, which remains under investigation, has not been established.

The departmental police commander for Santa Cruz, David Gómez, said investigators had information about the consultant's movements and deployed officers at the airport. He said a prior falling-out between the two was among the lines of inquiry. “Days ago Ms Beller and Mr Cerimedo are said to have had a relationship problem,” he said. The detainee was handed over to the Special Anti-Crime Force.

Security cameras recorded the attack, which took place on Monday night in the city's business district. Two men dressed as food delivery riders got off a motorcycle, shot Beller at the hotel entrance and took her bag and phone before fleeing. The 33-year-old lawyer underwent surgery and survived; none of the rounds struck vital organs. The case is being investigated as attempted femicide.

From hospital, Beller said she had been summoned to the location on a pretext linked to a legal case and that she feigned death to avoid being finished off. She accused Cerimedo of having tried to strangle her on two occasions since their relationship began in late 2025, said she is four weeks pregnant and requested protection. She also said she has knowledge of alleged corruption within President Rodrigo Paz's circle. No charges have been brought over any of these allegations and the government has not responded to them.

Government Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo called for “a serious and thorough investigation” and said that in Bolivia “nobody is above the law.” Vice-President Edman Lara described the episode as an attack “against life, democracy and freedom of expression.”

Cerimedo co-founded the digital outlet La Derecha Diario and took part in the social media strategy behind Javier Milei's 2023 presidential campaign. He also worked for Jair Bolsonaro and was investigated by Brazilian courts over the dissemination of claims of fraud in the 2022 elections, a case from which he was cleared. He advised Paz's campaign and retains a link to his government, although the Bolivian executive maintains he is not part of the state structure. In July, the then minister of the presidency, José Luis Lupo, said his consultancy is funded with external resources.

Beller stood as a candidate for the Movement Towards Socialism in 2019 and in recent years has worked as a political analyst critical of that party.

World.title: Sheinbaum, Carney discuss trade ahead of Trump’s tariff deadline for Canada
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade during a call on Thursday. Their conversation came exactly 50 days after the U.S. government announced it hadn’t agreed to renew the USMCA free trade pact “in its current form.”

A statement released by Carney’s office said that the “Prime Minister and the President discussed ongoing developments affecting North American trade” during Thursday’s call.

“They underscored the importance of renewing the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) as soon as possible to provide greater certainty for North American businesses and workers,” the statement said.

The USMCA, which superseded NAFTA in 2020 and reached a trilateral review deadline this year, is known as CUSMA in Canada and T-MEC (Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá) in Mexico.

The statement issued by the Canadian prime minister’s office said that Carney and Sheinbaum also discussed “the progress between Canada and Mexico on cross-border trade.”

“They emphasized that strong bilateral cooperation is essential to shared continental security and prosperity,” it said. “Prime Minister Carney and President Sheinbaum agreed to remain in close contact.”

Today, I spoke with President Sheinbaum. We discussed ongoing developments affecting North American trade. More on our call:https://t.co/AIvsggyndW — Mark Carney (@MarkJCarney) August 20, 2026

As of 3 p.m. Thursday, neither Sheinbaum nor her office had commented on the call with Carney.

Sheinbaum has stressed that Mexico, the United States and Canada could reach an agreement to extend the USMCA for an additional 16 years “at any time,” although the Trump administration has various concerns about the pact and its trade relationships with its neighbors, including ones related to trade deficits, energy policy and China.

The USMCA — which took effect when Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Donald Trump and Justin Trudeau were in office — governs trade worth around US $2 trillion annually. Even with the free-trade pact in place, Trump last year imposed tariffs on various Mexican and Canadian goods, including vehicles, steel and aluminum. In trade talks with U.S. officials, Mexico is seeking the reduction, or ideally the elimination, of the tariffs.

On Tuesday, Trump agreed to delay planned 50% tariffs on Canadian goods worth about $20 billion annually. However, the duties could take effect on Saturday if Canada doesn’t reach a deal with the U.S. before then.

Carney thanks Sheinbaum for Mexico’s support in combating wildfires in Canada

According to the Canadian government’s readout of Thursday’s call, Carney thanked Sheinbaum for “Mexico’s support in combating wildfires in Canada this summer, including through the deployment of more than 400 firefighters and support personnel.”

Mexican firefighters and technical personnel specializing in forest fires traveled to British Columbia earlier this month to support emergency efforts during intense wildfires in the western Canadian province.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Vietnam’s exports to Mexico double amid fears of Chinese tariff-dodging
World.content:
The value of Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first six months of 2026, raising suspicions that Chinese goods are being passed off as Vietnamese goods to avoid steep tariffs when entering the country.

According to Bank of Mexico data, Mexico imported products worth US $18.4 billion from Vietnam between January and June, an increase of 103% compared to the same period of 2025.

The value of imports from Vietnam in the first six months of the year was equivalent to 82% of Mexico’s total outlay on Vietnam-sourced products in 2025. Imports from the Southeast Asian country totaled a record high of $22.37 billion last year.

Bank of Mexico data shows that Mexico’s imports from Vietnam have increased significantly since 2010. Mexico’s outlay on products from Vietnam last year was almost 26 times higher than in 2010, when goods worth $836 million came into the country from the Southeast Asian nation.

Mexico’s main imports from Vietnam are currently tech products such as electronic circuits, telephones, computers and machinery parts, according to the news outlet Expansión.

The sharp increase in imports from Vietnam in the first six months of 2026 came after Mexico, on Jan. 1, imposed new and higher tariffs on goods from China and other countries with which it doesn’t have free trade agreements.

Vietnamese goods can enter Mexico tariff-free as both Vietnam and Mexico — along with 10 other countries including the United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and Australia — are signatories to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, or CPTPP for short.

Vietnamese or Chinese?

Expansión noted that if a Chinese product only goes to Vietnam to be relabeled as Vietnamese or to undergo “a minor process before arriving in Mexico,” it shouldn’t qualify for tariff-free status under CPTPP.

“The risk arises when customs controls don’t differentiate between legitimate [Vietnamese] manufacturing and insufficient transformation” of a Chinese product in Vietnam, Expansión reported.

The United States — which has imposed very high tariffs on imports from China during a long-running trade war with the East Asian nation — has identified Vietnam as a transshipment hub for Chinese goods. In “The Great Transshipment Scam,” a report published by the White House this month, Vietnam is listed among countries on “Tier 2” of a “shadow transshipment network.”

Countries are listed on “Tier 2” if they show “significant transshipment volumes combined with deeper integration into China-linked supply chains, input sourcing, manufacturing platforms, logistics systems, or regional rerouting channels.”

The same report identifies Mexico as a “Tier 1” country in the so-called “shadow transshipment network,” with “large absolute volumes of China-linked goods; diversified industrial bases and major U.S.-bound export platforms where transshipment risk is embedded within broad legitimate trade flows.”

The U.S. government’s argument is essentially that Mexico facilitates the tariff-free entry of Chinese goods to the United States. Given that Mexico imposed new and higher tariffs on imports from China this year — a move aimed at protecting Mexican industry but also widely seen as an attempt to placate the U.S. — Chinese exporters now have added incentive to route Mexico-bound goods through third countries that have free trade agreements with Mexico, such as Vietnam.

This practice — if it is indeed occurring — would undermine Mexico’s efforts to protect its domestic industries. Mexican industry, Expansión reported, is concerned about Chinese companies with export-oriented operations in Vietnam, even though many manufacturing companies that operate in Mexico use Chinese inputs due to their low cost, or because no alternatives are made locally or within the region.

In its report, the White House said that “every year, the United States loses tens of billions of dollars to the illegal transshipment of goods from higher-tariff countries through more than 40 lower-tariff jurisdictions before those goods enter the American market.”

“Historically, much of this activity has involved Chinese-origin goods,” the report added.

U.S. President Donald Trump has long accused Mexico of being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods that eventually enter the United States. Mexico has denied that claim.

Although Trump has imposed tariffs on various Mexican goods, including vehicles, steel and aluminum, the majority of Mexico’s exports to the U.S. enter that country tariff-free under the USMCA free trade pact. Mexico — where a significant number of Chinese companies have opened plants in recent years — is thus an attractive “back door” to the United States.

Meanwhile, the Vietnamese Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Vietnam would continue to address U.S. concerns about ​the transshipment of goods in a ‌constructive manner, according to Reuters.

With reports from Expansión

World.title: Mexico City launches drive to plant a million native trees in underserved boroughs by 2030
World.content:
Not regarded as one of the country’s top tree cities, Mexico City has begun an urban reforestation drive that aims to turn sidewalks, medians and other “gray” spaces into 1 million new shade points by 2030.

The program is built around the international 3-30-300 guideline: Residents should be able to see at least three trees from each window of their homes; all neighborhoods should include at least 30% tree canopy covering; and households should have a park or green area within 300 meters, about 1,000 feet.

Launched Tuesday by Mayor Clara Brugada at a housing complex in Iztacalco — which has the fewest trees of any of Mexico City’s 16 boroughs — the program calls for planting 200,000 native trees annually across the capital.

Officials said the plan calls for 100,000 trees to be planted this year, with priority for the eastern boroughs, where green-space shortages are most acute: Iztacalco, Iztapalapa, Venustiano Carranza, Gustavo A. Madero and Tláhuac.

The initiative will focus on streets, medians, sidewalks and other urban sites, separate from tree-planting efforts in nature, and neighborhood residents are expected to participate.

The project will rely on native species selected for their suitability to the capital’s climate and streets, such as having root systems that are less likely to damage sidewalks.

These include sweetgum, cazahuate, colorín (a coral tree), guaje, guamúchil, palo verde, ash, macuil and ceiba (also known as kapok).

The selected trees also don’t require a lot of maintenance, aren’t as vulnerable to pests and disease as nonnative ornamental trees, and can support air quality and pollination, Julia Álvarez Icaza, head of Mexico City’s Environment Ministry (Sedema), said in a press release.

The trees are expected to be young, nursery-grown saplings rather than mature or full-grown trees. “The tree will be the size of the child,” Brugada said in urging schoolchildren to care for a tree as it grows.

Brugada said the 1 million trees could capture at least 20,000 tons of carbon dioxide and remove pollutants equivalent to taking 4,000 cars off city streets annually. She also said that “where today [rain]water runs over cement, there will be soil that absorbs the water.”

The government plans neighborhood meetings before planting days to recruit residents to care for trees near their homes. Schools also will be invited to participate.

“We need to raise environmental awareness, and it is children and young people who are sometimes the most aware of the need to plant trees,” Brugada said.

With reports from El Universal, Chilango.com and Talla Política

World.title: Sinaloa capital’s Independence Day celebrations set to return after 2 years
World.content:
For the first time since 2023, the state of Sinaloa will stage Independence Day celebrations in Culiacán, its capital city, incuding the traditional public Grito.

Interim Governor Yeraldine Bonilla this week announced that the Grito will be celebrated in the Governor’s Palace Esplanade, declaring that preparations are already under way to resume the popular Sept. 15-16 festival and the massive celebrations that accompany it.

Culiacán’s “Grito” — an event that commemorates Father Miguel Hidalgo’s Sept. 16, 1810, call to arms which launched the initial insurrection of Mexico’s War for Independence — was canceled in 2024 and 2025 due to widespread cartel violence.

The cancellations were imposed because authorities were unable to contain a civil war that broke out within the Sinaloa Cartel in mid-2024. Local media reports indicate that there have been more than 3,700 violent deaths and nearly 4,300 people have been kidnapped and/or disappeared since the violence began.

State authorities preferred to prioritize public security, canceling the capital’s broader Independence Day festivities the past two years and opting for restricted civic ceremonies.

After telling reporters on Tuesday that “there will be an Independence Day celebration” next month, Bonilla said, “I hope to see you there,” encouraging Sinaloans “to get ready to celebrate” the Grito and to participate in the traditional patriotic revelry that accompanies it.

The governor said her administration is negotiating with several artists and entertainers, adding that the musical line-up will be announced in the coming weeks. Bonilla said organizers have been in contact with performers who were scheduled to appear at last year’s event, including El Coyote, Marisela and Miguel Bosé.

The Grito — or Cry for Independence — is celebrated in public squares across the country on the night of Sept 15, with a local official presiding over thronging crowds by ringing a bell and shouting out names of heroes, interspersed with cries of “¡Viva México!”

Sept. 16 typically features military and civic parades, street parties and cultural events. Sinaloa officials said they will release an official program for the Sept. 16 events in Culiacán by the end of the month.

By making the announcement, Bonilla confirmed that large civic events — including concerts and public celebrations — will gradually return to Culiacán’s public squares and plazas across the state.

With reports from Animal Político, Debate, Eje Central and Excelsior

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: A 2025 security snapshot
World.content:
On Aug. 13, the national statistics agency INEGI published the results of the 2026 National Census of Federal Public Security and National Census of State Public Security.

This “Mexico in Numbers” article looks at some of the key results. It also includes some of the security statistics presented by the federal government last week.

Security spending by National Guard and state forces exceeded 136 billion pesos in 2025

INEGI reported that the “total budget” exercised by the National Guard (GN) and state public security authorities in 2025 was 136.16 billion pesos (US $8 billion).

Just over one-fifth of that amount — 20.7% — was spent by the GN, while the remainder was used by security authorities in Mexico’s 31 states. (Security spending in Mexico City wasn’t included in the 2026 security census.)

INEGI said that using prices from the second quincena (15-day period) of July 2018 — i.e. before Mexico’s inflation rate spiked significantly in the early 2020s — spending by the GN and state security authorities last year amounted to 97.13 billion pesos.

That figure represented a 17.5% decrease compared to spending by the GN and state security authorities in 2024, although expenditure in Mexico City was included in the previous security census data.

Firearm seizures increased by more than 70% in 2025

INEGI reported that the National Guard and state security forces seized 21,088 firearms in 2025, an increase of 72.4% compared to the 12,232 guns they confiscated in 2024.

State security forces seized 12,910 firearms last year, representing 61.2% of the total. The National Guard confiscated 8,178 guns, representing 38.8% of the total.

The number of firearms seized by state security forces increased 36% annually from 9,490 in 2024.

Meanwhile, the year-over-year confiscations by the National Guard soared 198.2% from 2,742 in 2024.

The combined total of firearm seizures trended up in the past five years, but the increase in 2025 was easily the largest.

State authorities received more than 13.7 million emergency calls in 2025

INEGI reported that 13.74 million “emergency incidents” were reported to state security authorities in 2025 via calls to the “911 system.”

That number represented a 2.8% increase compared to 2024.

The GN and state security forces arrested more than 400,000 people in 2025

INEGI reported that in 2025, the National Guard and state security forces arrested 413,127 people were subsequently handed over to authorities. The number of arrests declined 4% compared to 2024.

In 2025, state security forces arrested 389,921 people, representing 94.4% of all detentions. The number of arrests made by state security forces declined 7.3% on a year-over-year basis.

The GN arrested 23,206 people in 2025, an increase of 137.4% compared to 2024.

INEGI detailed the reasons why some 413,000 people were arrested last year. It divided the causes into two categories: “alleged civic infractions” and “alleged crimes.”

The five most common civic infractions allegedly committed by people who were arrested in 2025 were:

Causing scandals or noise that threatens people’s tranquility and health: 71,227 arrests (17.2% of the total) Consuming drugs on the street or in other public places: 33,838 arrests (8.2%) Consuming alcoholic beverages on the street or in other public places: 33,180 arrests (8%) Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs: 15,569 arrests (3.8%) Preventing the use of public roads or restricting the freedom of movement of

people without just cause (e.g. protesting on the street without “just cause”): 12,518 arrests (3%)

The five most common crimes allegedly committed by people who were arrested in 2025 were:

Small-scale drug trafficking: 66,968 arrests (16.2% of the total) Robbery: 28,178 arrests (6.8%) Crimes involving weapons, explosives and other “destructive materials”: 9,704 arrests (2.3%) Assault: 9,701 arrests (2.3%) Crimes involving weapons and “prohibited objects”: 7,615 arrests (1.8%)

In 2025, the National Guard and state security authorities arrested 2,869 people for allegedly committing homicides. Murder was the ninth most common crime for which people were arrested in Mexico last year.

The federal government’s monthly ‘security census’

Federal security officials provide their own “security census,” of sorts, on a monthly basis at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s weekday morning press conferences.

Here is a recap of the statistics presented on Aug. 11.

There were 10,309 homicides across Mexico in the first seven months of 2026. The daily murder rate between January and July was 48.6, a reduction of 30.8% compared to the same period of 2025.

Between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and July 31, 2026, authorities arrested 63,564 people for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as murder, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

Authorities seized 518.7 tonnes of drugs between October 2024 and July 2026.

The Mexican military dismantled 2,725 clandestine drug laboratories between October 2024 and July 2026.

World.title: Mexico refuses to support US-led push to address Nicaragua’s election ban
World.content:
Mexico abstained from voting on a United States proposal for an emergency meeting of the Organization of American States (OAS) on how to respond to Nicaragua’s decision to bar opposition politicians from running for office.

Despite Mexico’s objections, the OAS on Wednesday approved a resolution summoning foreign ministers to an emergency council session by a lopsided 29-1 vote. The OAS is the leading international political forum for Western Hemisphere nations.

Brazil was the lone “nay” vote, while Haiti and Venezuela were absent. Nicaragua, which withdrew from the OAS in 2023, was also absent.

The resolution — which invokes Articles in the OAS Charter that demand a collective response — defines developments in Nicaragua as “a problem of an urgent nature and of common interest to the American States.”

Alejandro Encinas, Mexico’s representative to the OAS, said Mexico does not consider it appropriate to characterize Nicaragua’s internal situation as a threat to regional peace or security.

He warned that doing so could open the door to actions that exceed the OAS’s authority, describing these potential actions as “incompatible with the principles of respect for sovereignty, self-determination of peoples, non-intervention and peaceful settlement of disputes.”

Encinas also argued that treating an internal political crisis as a security issue does not necessarily help resolve it. On the contrary, he said, it can generate confrontation, deepen isolation and lead to measures that hinder a peaceful solution and produce greater destabilization.

The OAS action came in response to Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega’s vow to end elections and to promote constitutional amendments aimed at blocking opposition figures from power. Ortega announced the decision in July at the anniversary of the country’s Sandanista Revolution, which first brought him into power in 1979.

Argentina, Panama, Paraguay and Uruguay joined the United States in advancing this week’s measure — titled “Convocation of a Meeting of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs to Consider the Situation in Nicaragua” — at an Aug. 5 special session of the Permanent Council.

The U.S. insists the emergency meeting must take place before Sept. 1, when the Ortega regime is set to codify its latest policy reforms, including the suspension of future elections.

The OAS as a bloc cannot impose economic or trade sanctions on a country, limiting itself to diplomatic condemnation or suspension of a member state or recommending that its members punish a nation that violates democratic norms.

With reports from Animal Político, EWTN News, Al Jazeera and Buenos Aires Times

World.title: Sheinbaum unveils Olinia Carga, a Mexican-made electric cargo vehicle: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🚗 Government presents Olinia Carga, its second EV prototype: The light-cargo vehicle, unveiled 11 weeks after the Olinia 1 prototype, can carry up to 650 kg and has a range of over 120 km. Olinia will launch a public tender for private-sector partners, with Olinia Carga set to go on sale in late 2027 for around 150,000 pesos.

Government presents Olinia Carga, its second EV prototype: The light-cargo vehicle, unveiled 11 weeks after the Olinia 1 prototype, can carry up to 650 kg and has a range of over 120 km. Olinia will launch a public tender for private-sector partners, with Olinia Carga set to go on sale in late 2027 for around 150,000 pesos. 🚔 New arrest in “El Mayo” Zambada kidnapping case: Fausto Corrales Rodríguez, who allegedly accompanied former Culiacán mayor Héctor Cuén to the meeting where Zambada was kidnapped in July 2024, was arrested in Mexico City. Sheinbaum said the arrest was “important” and could help clarify what happened that day.

New arrest in “El Mayo” Zambada kidnapping case: Fausto Corrales Rodríguez, who allegedly accompanied former Culiacán mayor Héctor Cuén to the meeting where Zambada was kidnapped in July 2024, was arrested in Mexico City. Sheinbaum said the arrest was “important” and could help clarify what happened that day. 🇦🇷 ✈️ Navy officer’s extradition delayed by legal issue: Sheinbaum said Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a huachicol fiscal network and arrested in Argentina in April, raised a legal matter there that delayed his transfer to Mexico. She added that officials told her his extradition “is not in doubt.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

A prototype of a new Olinia electric vehicle was unveiled at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Thursday morning press conference. The presentation of Olinia Carga — a light-cargo vehicle — came around 11 weeks after the government debuted a prototype of Olinia 1, a small car.

The Olinia project is an initiative of the Sheinbaum administration. The aim is to produce, in conjunction with private sector partners, electric vehicles that are more affordable than EVs that are currently available in the Mexican market.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about a new arrest linked to the 2024 kidnapping of Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada. The president also commented on the expected extradition to Mexico of a Mexican Navy officer who was arrested in Argentina earlier this year in connection with a fuel smuggling/tax evasion (huachicol fiscal) scheme.

Government presents prototype of second Olinia vehicle

At the start of the press conference, Sheinbaum noted that officials and reporters were gathered in the courtyard of the National Palace “because today we’re presenting Olinia Carga — the second Olinia model.”

“… Olinia, as you’ll remember, is a project that began when we came to government and the objective is to promote mini-electromobility in our country,” she said.

An Olinia Carga prototype — loaded with wooden crates filled with flowers — was unveiled a short time later.

#Mañanera | 🚗Roberto Capuano, quien encabeza el proyecto Olinia, detalla que el nuevo vehículo, llamado “Olinia Carga”, está diseñado como transporte de mercancías, con una capacidad de carga de más de 600 kilos y espacio para transportar “muchísimas cosas”, entre ellas, hasta… pic.twitter.com/DohfUQtXEg — El Universal (@El_Universal_Mx) August 20, 2026

Roberto Capuano, director of the Olinia project, told reporters that the Olinia Carga is “a vehicle designed for work.”

“To design it, we went to see how cargo is moved in our towns and cities,” he said.

“… Small businesses use private cars, which weren’t designed for work, or motorbikes, which limit the volume [of cargo that can be moved],” Capuano said.

He said that small businesses in Mexico need “something compact, low-cost and designed for work” to move cargo.

“In this space, our second vehicle was born,” Capuano said.

He said that Olinia Carga has the capacity to transport cargo weighing up to 650 kilograms. Its range is more than 120 kilometers, Capuano said.

“It’s designed to hold a lot of things, including one of the most common cargo units in Mexico, which is the wooden crate,” he said.

“Twelve wooden crates fit on the [vehicle’s] bed, and they can be stacked on multiple levels,” Capuano said.

He also noted that the vehicle has “what we call a low trunk.”

As the Olinia Carga is an electric vehicle, “the space below the bed is empty,” Capuano said.

That space, he said, can be used to transport additional items such as folding furniture, which can be used to set up an outdoor stall. Capuano noted that two people can travel “comfortably” in the vehicle.

He said that the Olinia project has shown that “in Mexico we can design and develop technological products for our own needs.”

“Now, the next step is to become a company capable of making, distributing and selling these vehicles across the entire country,” Capuano said.

“For that reason, … we’re going to launch a public tender to select our strategic allies,” he said, explaining that Mexican and foreign companies will be eligible to participate.

“… What we’re mainly looking for is not money, … what we’re seeking is industrial and commercial capacity,” Capuano said.

The Olinia chief said that Olinia 1 is slated to go on sale in the summer of next year, while Olinia Carga will be available starting in late 2027. He said that Olinia Carga will be sold for around 150,000 pesos (US $8,800). Olinia 1 is set to be sold for the same price.

New arrest in connection with the kidnapping of ‘El Mayo’

A reporter raised the arrest in Mexico City on Wednesday of Fausto Corrales Rodríguez, who allegedly accompanied former Culiacán mayor Héctor Cuén to a meeting at which “El Mayo” Zambada was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López in July 2024.

Zambada was subsequently forced onto a private plane and flown to New Mexico, where he and Guzmán López — a son of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán — were arrested by U.S. authorities on July 25, 2024.

Cuén was murdered the same day and Corrales is alleged to have given false information to authorities about the homicide.

La #FGRInforma al Pueblo de México la

aprehensión de Fausto “N”, posible implicado en el caso del secuestro de Ismael “N”, llevado a cabo en julio de 2024. Más información ▶️ https://t.co/CXBxs0OTQv pic.twitter.com/rJDSkMFete — FGR México (@FGRMexico) August 19, 2026

The reporter asked the president whether the arrest of Corrales would help uncover more information about Zambada’s “transfer” to the United States.

“This arrest is important,” Sheinbaum said.

She said she expected that Corrales’ statements to authorities would help shed light on what happened in Sinaloa on the day that Zambada was kidnapped, an event that caused a major escalation in a long-running battle between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos, rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel.

Sheinbaum: Fernando Farías’ extradition to Mexico is delayed due to a legal issue

A reporter asked the president whether she had received any information about the transfer to Mexico of Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, who was arrested in Buenos Aires in April. Farías, a nephew of former Navy Minister José Rafael Ojeda Durán, is accused of leading a huachicol fiscal network.

Sheinbaum said she had been informed by government officials that Farías “raised a legal matter in Argentina and for that reason his arrival in Mexico was delayed.”

She said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office would provide more information about the suspect’s extradition to Mexico.

“Today in the Security Cabinet [meeting], representatives of the attorney general told us that his transfer to Mexico is not in doubt,” Sheinbaum added.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Is Mexico really dangerous? Why travel advisories don’t tell the whole story
World.content:
If you’ve ever mentioned an upcoming trip to a friend or family member, chances are someone’s told you to “check the travel advisory.”

And they’re not wrong.

Travel advisories exist for a reason. They can provide genuinely important information about crime, political unrest, natural disasters, health concerns and other risks that could affect your trip.

But there’s a problem with the way we sometimes use them. We treat a travel advisory as though it were a map, but it isn’t. It’s more of a compass. It can point you toward areas where you need to pay attention, but it can’t tell you what life looks like on every street, in every city or for every traveler.

A vast country of distinct realities

Mexico is a perfect example of why context matters.

Mexico is enormous. It’s a country full of numerous different realities. It stretches from the Pacific to the Caribbean, from deserts in the north to tropics in the south, with sprawling cities, tiny mountain villages, beach communities, agricultural regions and everything in between.

So, when someone asks me, “But isn’t Mexico dangerous?” my first question is usually, “Where in Mexico?” Because that’s a very different question.

I live in Bucerías, just outside of Puerto Vallarta, but I’ve also traveled the country extensively. Places like Guanajuato, Guadalajara, León, Puebla and Mexico City each have their own personalities, challenges and rhythms.

Walking around a busy neighborhood in Mexico City isn’t the same experience as traveling through a remote rural area. The concerns you might have visiting one state may be completely irrelevant in another. Yet when someone sees a headline about crime or a government advisory warning about Mexico, the entire country suddenly becomes one giant red zone in their imagination.

That’s not really how countries work, though.

Imagine issuing a single travel warning for the United States based on what happens in Chicago, New Orleans, Detroit or a particular border region, and then applying that warning equally to someone visiting a small town in Vermont. It wouldn’t make much sense.

The same principle applies to Mexico.

Broad tools rather than local guides

Government advisories are deliberately cautious, and they should be. The U.S., U.K., Canada, Australia and other governments have systems designed to warn their citizens about potential risks abroad. Those warnings can be incredibly useful, particularly when there’s a serious and immediate threat. But they’re broad tools. They aren’t designed to tell you whether the café you’re planning to visit is safe, whether the neighborhood around your hotel feels comfortable or whether a demonstration taking place hundreds of kilometers away is likely to affect your weekend.

That’s where the rest of your research comes in.

A national warning should be the beginning of the conversation, not the end of it.

If an advisory makes you nervous, don’t simply cancel the trip. Dig a little deeper. Look at the specific region you’re visiting. Many governments provide much more detailed information once you get beyond the headline.

Check local news and see what’s actually happening in the city or state you’re planning to visit. Talk to people who live there or have recently traveled there, and check embassy or consulate notices for local developments, demonstrations, weather events or transportation disruptions.

It’s also worth thinking about the kind of traveler you are. Someone traveling alone through a remote region with little Spanish and limited access to transportation has a very different risk profile from someone staying in an established tourist area with reliable transport and plenty of local support.

Neither is necessarily right or wrong. They’re simply different.

Acknowledging risk without assuming danger

Living here has made me much more aware of the difference between acknowledging risk and assuming danger. It’s taught me to look at the whole picture.

Crime exists in Mexico. Of course it does. So do hurricanes, earthquakes, protests, road accidents, medical emergencies and all the other things that can go wrong when you’re traveling anywhere. But those realities don’t automatically define every person’s experience.

I’d never tell anyone to ignore an official warning. Quite the opposite. If multiple governments are warning against travel to a particular region because of serious, ongoing threats, pay attention. If there are reports of targeted attacks, widespread unrest or a major natural disaster, that’s not the moment to decide you’re going to prove everyone wrong. Being adventurous doesn’t require being reckless. But neither does being cautious require being afraid of an entire country.

Why government advice varies

One thing I’ve always found interesting is comparing travel advisories from different countries. They don’t always say exactly the same thing. That’s not necessarily because one is right and another is wrong. Governments have different thresholds, different information and different approaches to risk.

If several governments are highlighting the same specific threat, that’s certainly worth taking seriously. If their advice differs considerably, though, that’s a reason to investigate further.

The goal isn’t to find the advisory that tells you what you want to hear. It’s to understand why the advice differs.

Practical details and insurance fine print

There are also plenty of risks that have nothing to do with crime, so don’t dismiss the practical stuff. What will the weather be like? Are there hurricanes or extreme heat at that time of year? How good is medical care where you’re going? Will you have reliable transportation? Are there areas where cell service is limited? What happens if you get sick or stranded?

And check your travel insurance. That one is particularly important because some policies have exclusions related to government travel warnings. A destination being somewhere you can travel doesn’t necessarily mean your insurance will cover you if you’re traveling against official advice. So read the fine print before you need it.

Informed decisions over absolute fear

There’s no such thing as completely risk-free travel. There isn’t even such a thing as a completely risk-free life. We accept a certain amount of risk every time we get into a car, cross a road, fly somewhere or try something unfamiliar. Travel is about managing that risk intelligently rather than pretending it doesn’t exist.

Places change. Situations change. Advisories change. That’s why context matters.

A destination that appears in a warning today may look very different six months or a year from now. And a country that’s broadly considered safe can still contain places where travelers should exercise considerable caution. The important thing is knowing the difference.

So yes, check the travel advisory. Please do! But then keep reading to better understand the risks that apply to you, rather than simply the risks attached to an entire country.

Travel advisories are there to help us make informed decisions, not to make those decisions for us. Let them point you toward the questions you need to ask, because being a smart traveler isn’t about eliminating every possible risk. It’s about understanding where the risks are, preparing for them and making an informed decision about whether the experience is worth it.

And sometimes, once you’ve looked beyond the headline, you discover something quite wonderful. The place you were warned about isn’t necessarily the place you imagined. It’s a real place, filled with real people, complicated realities, beautiful moments and stories you never would have found on a government website.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Snow Has Hit 26,000 Bolivian Families, and a River Took Out a Yungas Town
World.content:
Bolivia · Economy

Key Facts 26,202 families affected and 6,211 classed as damnificadas, across 274 communities in 75 municipalities.

and 6,211 classed as damnificadas, across 274 communities in 75 municipalities. Three departments: Potosí, Oruro and La Paz. Potosí is the epicentre and has declared a regional emergency.

Potosí, Oruro and La Paz. Potosí is the epicentre and has declared a regional emergency. The main driver is snowfall and cold , not rain — a normal altiplano winter phenomenon at an abnormal intensity.

, not rain — a normal altiplano winter phenomenon at an abnormal intensity. Separately, at Quime in La Paz, the Kuyuma river burst its banks on 18–19 August, flooding homes and tearing up street platforms.

in La Paz, the Kuyuma river burst its banks on 18–19 August, flooding homes and tearing up street platforms. No declaration yet at Quime. The municipality is assembling the technical file needed to request state aid.

The municipality is assembling the technical file needed to request state aid. An excavator was trapped in the river at Quime — a meaningful loss for a municipality with almost no heavy plant.

Two different kinds of bad weather are hitting western Bolivia at once, and the smaller one is doing the most visible damage.

The Bolivia weather emergency now running across the west of the country is really two events with one number attached. The big one is snow and cold across Potosí, Oruro and La Paz, which the Vice-Ministry of Civil Defence says has affected 26,202 families. The small one is a river in a yungas town called Quime, which took out streets and homes on 18 and 19 August and is what the pictures are of.

La Paz beneath Illimani. Snow and cold have affected families across three departments. (Photo internet reproduction)

The number, and what is behind it

Civil Defence, through vice-minister Roberto Rivero, reported on 19 August that 26,202 families had been affected and 6,211 classed as damnificadas — a Bolivian category covering severe impact, including loss of livelihood, not only uninhabitable housing. The damage spans 274 communities in 75 municipalities across Potosí, Oruro and La Paz. A separate wire count the same day gave 26,220 families and 323 communities, which is the usual spread you get on a moving emergency.

The driver is snowfall and cold, with Potosí — the Uyuni area in particular — worst hit. Potosí has declared a regional emergency. This is a winter event on the altiplano, where snow is normal and this quantity of it is not.

The economic damage from snow in this part of Bolivia is mostly livestock and roads: llamas and sheep lost, pasture buried, and highland routes closed for days at a time.

What happened at Quime

Quime sits in Inquisivi province in La Paz department, on the fringe where the high Andes drop into the yungas. Intense rainfall pushed the Kuyuma river over its banks on 18 and 19 August. Water entered homes, street platforms were eroded, debris was carried through the town and services were cut.

The municipality has not declared an emergency. It is preparing the technical file that would let it request state assistance, which is the step that determines whether machinery arrives or does not. In the meantime it is doing what it can — channelling the river, clearing material and trying to put the bed back where it was.

The detail that tells you the most is the excavator trapped in the water. Municipalities here typically own one or two pieces of heavy plant. Losing one to the river is not a colourful aside; it is a large share of the town’s capacity to dig itself out.

The La Paz governor’s office lists Quime alongside La Asunta, Luribay, Palca and Yanacachi among the worst-affected municipalities. At Palca the road platform is expected to need about a month of repair work, and the national roads agency has been clearing snow at La Cumbre, the pass above the capital.

Why the seasonality matters

Senamhi, the national weather service, dates the altiplano rainy season from November to March. Snow in August is unremarkable; a rainfall-driven riada in August is not.

That distinction is worth holding on to, because coverage of Bolivian weather emergencies routinely runs the two together. The 26,202 figure is a snow-and-cold count for three departments. The Quime flood is a rain event in one municipality. Neither number describes the other.

It also matters for what comes next. If the rains have arrived early in the yungas, the wet season that normally starts in November has a long way to run, and the roads that were damaged this week will be tested again.

What a Bolivia weather emergency costs a country like this one

Bolivia is having an unusually good year on paper. Mining exports reached US$4.45 billion in the first half, up 91% on a year earlier, and the gap between the official and parallel dollar has all but closed after two years of shortage. None of that reaches Quime.

Rural road damage is where weather turns into economics here. The yungas grow coffee, citrus and coca, and they are the corridor between La Paz and the lowlands. When the roads go, produce does not reach market, prices in the city move, and the repair bill lands on municipalities with almost no budget.

Emergency response also costs hard currency — machinery, spare parts, fuel — and Bolivia has spent two years rationing exactly that. A good export half-year does not build a bridge in Inquisivi, and nothing in the current budget suggests one is coming.

What to watch, and what to do

Whether the national government moves from Civil Defence coordination to formal declarations with budget attached. In Bolivia that step is what converts sympathy into equipment.

Whether more municipalities follow Potosí into regional emergency. The count of affected families has been rising through the week.

And practically: if you are travelling in the La Paz yungas or across the altiplano in the coming weeks, check road status before setting out rather than on the way. Landslides and snow closures in this terrain shut routes for days, and the detours are long. La Cumbre, the pass every road out of La Paz to the north crosses, is the one to check first.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people are affected by the Bolivia weather emergency? Civil Defence reported 26,202 families affected and 6,211 classed as damnificadas across 274 communities in 75 municipalities of Potosí, Oruro and La Paz. Those totals are driven mainly by snowfall and cold, not by flooding. What happened at Quime? Intense rain pushed the Kuyuma river over its banks on 18 and 19 August, flooding homes in the town centre, eroding street platforms and cutting services. An excavator was trapped in the river. The municipality has not declared an emergency but is preparing a file to request state aid. Is this normal for August in Bolivia? Snowfall on the altiplano in August is normal, though not at this intensity. Heavy rain driving a river over its banks is not — Senamhi dates the altiplano rainy season from November to March.

Sources: Viceministerio de Defensa Civil de Bolivia; Gobernación de La Paz; Senamhi Bolivia

World.title: Chile Wants Six Million Tonnes of Copper. Right Now It Is Producing Less Each Year
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts The target. Mining and economy minister Daniel Mas says Chile should return to about six million tonnes of copper a year.

Mining and economy minister Daniel Mas says Chile should return to about six million tonnes of copper a year. Where it is now. Output has been stuck between 5 and 5.5 million tonnes; Chile produced 5,415,200 tonnes in 2025, down 1.65% on 2024.

Output has been stuck between 5 and 5.5 million tonnes; Chile produced 5,415,200 tonnes in 2025, down 1.65% on 2024. The direction of travel. Cochilco expects 5.27 million tonnes in 2026 — a fall of 2.6%.

Cochilco expects 5.27 million tonnes in 2026 — a fall of 2.6%. The instrument. A framework law on sectoral authorisations aims to cut permitting times by 30% to 70%.

A framework law on sectoral authorisations aims to cut permitting times by 30% to 70%. The pipeline. Sixteen mining projects worth more than US$24 billion have entered environmental review since March, over 83% of all investment being assessed nationally.

Sixteen mining projects worth more than US$24 billion have entered environmental review since March, over 83% of all investment being assessed nationally. The long view. Cochilco’s current projection peaks at 6.06 million tonnes in 2033, after a trough of 5.43 million in 2030.

The government has a number, a permitting law and a pipeline. What it does not yet have is a year in which output stops falling.

The Chile copper production target everyone is now converging on is six million tonnes a year — the title of a Clapes UC seminar on 13 August, where mining and economy minister Daniel Mas said the country could reach it. It is a serious ambition from a government that has moved quickly on permitting. It also sits awkwardly next to Chile’s own forecast, which says output will fall this year.

An open pit in northern Chile. Output is forecast to fall 2.6% this year. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Chile copper production target versus the tape

Chile produced 5,415,200 tonnes of fine copper in 2025, down 1.65% on the year before. Cochilco, the state copper commission, expects 5.27 million tonnes in 2026, a decline of 2.6%, before a rebound to about 5.55 million in 2027. Mas himself has described output as stuck between 5 and 5.5 million tonnes a year, against a peak of 5.8 million in 2018.

So six million represents roughly a 14% increase on where the country is heading this year. Cochilco’s current ten-year projection does not get there at all: it sees output recovering to about 5.97 million tonnes in 2027, falling to a trough of 5.43 million in 2030 as existing deposits are depleted, peaking at 6.06 million in 2033 and easing to 5.86 million in 2034.

That is not an argument against the target. It is an argument about the timetable. Copper mines take between seven and twelve years to move from decision to first production, which means the tonnes that would meet a six-million goal are being decided now, not mined now.

What the government is actually changing

The centrepiece is Law 21.770, the framework law on sectoral authorisations, passed under the previous government in late 2025 and projected to cut permitting times by between 30% and 70%. Implementing it now falls to the Kast administration. In a country where a large mine can spend a decade in evaluation, that is the single most valuable thing a ministry can offer an investor.

Alongside it, the mining ministry is reworking the regulations on mine safety and on closure and tailings, moving some procedures to sworn declarations rather than full applications. It has also convened a technical group on exploration, aimed at junior miners’ access to risk capital and at reducing the permit load on early-stage work.

Exploration is the quiet part of this that matters most. Chile has not made a world-class copper discovery in years, and juniors — the small companies that do most of the world’s discovery work — have largely gone elsewhere.

The pipeline is real

Since the government took office in March, sixteen mining projects worth more than US$24 billion have entered the environmental assessment system. That is more than 83% of all investment currently under environmental review in Chile, which tells you both how large mining is in the economy and how thin everything else is.

Cochilco’s 2025–2034 investment portfolio runs to about US$104.5 billion, the largest in more than a decade. The CBC construction body counts US$87.7 billion of investment projects with defined schedules for 2026 to 2030, with 41% of that in mining.

There is also the Chile–Argentina mining integration treaty, revived this year, which the government estimates could unlock more than US$20.7 billion of investment and add around 540,000 tonnes of annual copper output from deposits that straddle the border.

Why the target matters to you

If you live in Chile, copper is the exchange rate, the tax base and a large part of the current account. The peso traded around 926 to the US dollar on 20 August, pushed weaker on the day by a jump in oil prices. Two days earlier the central bank had reported that GDP fell 0.2% year on year in the second quarter — a second consecutive negative quarter, with mining a principal drag.

That is the loop the government is trying to break. Falling output means weaker growth, which means less revenue, which means more pressure on the copper royalty, which makes investment decisions harder. Adding tonnes is the only exit that does not involve raising taxes or cutting spending.

If you are invested in the sector, the number to track is not the target. It is the environmental assessment queue. Sixteen projects entering review is a leading indicator; approvals two to three years from now are what turn into tonnes at the end of the decade.

What could go wrong

Three things, in order of probability. Water, first: most Chilean copper is in the driest place on earth, and desalination adds cost to every project. Community consent, second: faster permits do not make opposition disappear, they concentrate it into a shorter window. And grade, third — Chilean ore is getting poorer, which means moving more rock for the same metal.

None of these is new, and none is solved by legislation. What legislation can do is stop good projects dying in a queue, which is a real and worthwhile thing.

The honest read is that Chile can probably get back toward six million tonnes, and on its own agency’s numbers not before the 2030s — and even then only by roughly a hundred thousand tonnes. A government that says so plainly will find the goal easier to defend than one that implies it is close.

What is the Chile copper production target? About six million tonnes a year. It was the framing of a Clapes UC seminar on 13 August 2026, where mining and economy minister Daniel Mas said Chile could reach it. Chile produced 5,415,200 tonnes in 2025. Is Chilean copper output rising? Not this year. Cochilco expects 5.27 million tonnes in 2026, a fall of 2.6% on 2025, before a rebound to about 5.55 million in 2027. Its ten-year projection peaks at 6.06 million tonnes in 2033. What is the government doing about it? A framework law on sectoral authorisations intended to cut permitting times by 30% to 70%, simpler mine safety and closure regulations, and a technical group on exploration financing. Sixteen mining projects worth over US$24 billion have entered environmental review since March.

Sources: Clapes UC — mining seminar; Cochilco — investment portfolio and forecasts; Ministerio de Minería de Chile

World.title: One Infected Cow in Sonora Lands Days Before the US Reopens Its Cattle Border
World.content:
Mexico · Business

Key Facts First case in Sonora since 1980. Senasica confirmed screwworm in a bovine at Munihuasa, in the Álamos municipality in the south of the state.

Senasica confirmed screwworm in a bovine at Munihuasa, in the Álamos municipality in the south of the state. Nationally. Senasica counted 1,969 active cases in epidemiological week 33, up from 1,818 on 8 August.

Senasica counted 1,969 active cases in epidemiological week 33, up from 1,818 on 8 August. The response. A 20-kilometre sanitary cordon, 360,000 sterile flies released and preventive treatment.

A 20-kilometre sanitary cordon, 360,000 sterile flies released and preventive treatment. The timing. The staged US reopening of Mexican cattle exports was set to begin on 24 August at Agua Prieta, crossing into Douglas, Arizona, with Santa Teresa and Columbus in New Mexico to follow.

The staged US reopening of Mexican cattle exports was set to begin on 24 August at Agua Prieta, crossing into Douglas, Arizona, with Santa Teresa and Columbus in New Mexico to follow. Why Sonora. The USDA had classed Sonora and Chihuahua as its lowest-risk Mexican states, citing established inspection programmes and distance from the southern outbreak.

The USDA had classed Sonora and Chihuahua as its lowest-risk Mexican states, citing established inspection programmes and distance from the southern outbreak. The volumes. Ranchers’ body CNOG expects about 700 head a day at the start, rising to 1,300–1,500 a day and roughly 40,000 a month through Sonora — against a pre-closure trade of about 1.26 million head a year.

Sonora was chosen as the low-risk state to restart cattle exports. Then it found its first case.

The first Sonora screwworm case in 46 years could hardly have arrived at a worse moment. Mexican animal health authority Senasica confirmed the parasite in a bovine at Munihuasa, in the Álamos municipality of southern Sonora — the state the United States had picked as one of two lowest-risk places to restart cattle exports from 24 August.

A feedlot in the US southwest. Mexican cattle exports have been shut for fourteen months. (Photo internet reproduction)

What was found, and where

Senasica reported one active case in Sonora, in a bovine at Munihuasa, in the municipality of Álamos, about 17 kilometres from the Chihuahua state line. It was announced on 19 August. Nationally, Senasica counted 1,969 active cases in epidemiological week 33, up from 1,818 on 8 August, so a single animal is statistically trivial. Geographically it is not.

Sonora borders Arizona. Until this detection it was one of only three Mexican states with no confirmed screwworm, and it had been officially free of the parasite since 1981, with no case since May 1980. It is now the thirtieth of thirty-two states to record one, leaving only Baja California and Baja California Sur clean. The US Department of Agriculture had identified Sonora, alongside Chihuahua, as a lowest-risk origin for resuming imports — on the strength of its inspection programme and its distance from the southern outbreak rather than simply its case count.

The state response was immediate: a 20-kilometre sanitary cordon around the detection, the release of 360,000 sterile flies, and preventive treatment of animals in the zone with doramectin for adults and a topical product on newborn calves’ umbilical cords. Governor Alfonso Durazo announced the case; the state agriculture secretary, Juan González, set out the technical response.

Why sterile flies

The New World screwworm is a fly whose larvae feed on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals. It was eradicated from North America decades ago using the sterile insect technique: mass-rearing male flies, sterilising them with radiation, and releasing them so that wild females mate without producing offspring.

It works, and it is slow. Each release only suppresses the generation it meets, so the flies have to keep coming until the wild population collapses. Mexico’s flies come from a plant at Metapa de Domínguez in Chiapas, opened by President Sheinbaum in June, which started at 28 million flies a week and is aiming for 100 million a week by the end of the year. The scale needed to hold a barrier across a country the size of Mexico is enormous.

This is why one case in Sonora is treated as an emergency rather than a veterinary footnote. The economic damage comes not from the animal but from what the detection does to the border.

What the border closure has already cost

The suspension of Mexican cattle exports has been expensive. Estimates of the damage range from about US$1.1 billion in income not received by ranchers to roughly US$2.4 billion in lost foreign exchange, depending on which industry figure you take and what period it covers.

The reopening was never going to restore that quickly. CNOG, the national ranchers’ body, expects about 700 head a day at the start, rising to 1,300–1,500 a day, and roughly 40,000 a month through Sonora from September — a fraction of the pre-closure trade, which ran to about 1.26 million head a year worth some US$1.2 billion.

Feedlots and packers on the US side have spent a year sourcing elsewhere. On the Mexican side, ranchers have been carrying animals they cannot sell across a border that has been fully shut for fourteen months and disrupted since November 2024. Roughly 1.7 million head have not crossed.

What the Sonora screwworm case does to the timetable

As of 20 August the staged reopening at Agua Prieta–Douglas was still scheduled for 24 August. Whether it holds is a USDA decision, and the department has moved quickly in both directions before.

The argument for proceeding is that the case is contained, cordoned and being treated, and that a single detection in a state the size of Sonora does not change the risk profile of the specific ranches approved to export. Sonora’s regional cattlemen’s union has publicly urged the USDA to hold the date. The argument against is that a state that has just lost a 45-year clean record is a strange place to restart a trade that was suspended over exactly this parasite.

For anyone with exposure to the cattle trade — ranchers, feedlots, packers, or investors in Mexican or US protein companies — the next few days are the ones that matter. A delay would push the restart past the end of August and into a market that has already repriced beef on the assumption of tight supply.

And for anyone simply living in northern Mexico or the US southwest, the practical point is smaller but real: livestock movement controls, inspections at internal checkpoints, and, if you travel with animals, paperwork that did not exist two years ago.
