World.title: Man jailed for chainsaw torment of teenager in shipping container
World.content:
A Tasmanian man who left a teenager tied up in a locked shipping container, threatened him with a chainsaw to his neck and later told the boy's father, "you'll never see your son again" if supposedly stolen items weren't returned, a court has heard.

WARNING: This story contains details of violence that some readers may find distressing

On Friday, Wayne Michael Ludbey, 32, was jailed for what the judge described as "premeditated violence carried out for vindictive reasons".

Ludbey pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Tasmania in Burnie to two counts of assault for the 2023 attack on the 17-year-old, which started around midday on September 12.

During sentencing, Justice Tamara Jago said that, despite the guilty plea, she did not accept that Ludbey had demonstrated remorse or shown insight into the seriousness of his crimes.

Boy restrained, bashed, sprayed with hose

The court heard that Ludbey believed the teenager had been stealing from the shipping container on his property at Strahan on Tasmania's West Coast.

Justice Jago told the court that on the day, Ludbey saw the boy and believed he was wearing work boots stolen from the container.

Ludbey then texted his wife: "I'm waiting for him, I'm going to get him".

About half an hour later, Ludbey confronted the teenager on the street and began assaulting him and attempted to force him into his nearby vehicle.

Ludbey saw the boy walking in Strahan on the day of the incident, the court heard. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Ludbey's younger brother Brady Ludbey then joined him in the attack, helping force the teenager into the car and allowing his elder brother to return to the driver's seat.

The younger brother was previously sentenced for his lesser part in the assault.

Justice Jago told the court Ludbey then drove the teenager to his property, accused him of the theft and demanded that his belongings be returned.

"The complainant had no idea what you were talking about, nor why you were accusing him," the judge said.

Brothers who kidnapped, menaced teen with chainsaw lashed by judge A teenage boy was "terrified" during an assault by two brothers, during which he was kidnapped and menaced with a chainsaw in a shipping container in Tasmania.

At the shipping container, the assault continued and the Ludbey brothers restrained the teenager with straps and zip ties bound around his hands and legs.

Ludbey then started a chainsaw, revved it, and held the chain against the boy's neck while it was not moving.

He then bashed the boy with a piece of wood to his arms and head, causing several injuries.

After spraying the boy with a hose, Ludbey and his younger brother locked the container with a chain and padlock, leaving the boy tied up inside.

"You left him trapped, wet, restrained and undoubtedly very frightened," Justice Jago said.

The judge said a short time later that Ludbey, who had possession of the boy's phone, called the boy's father from it and issued the ultimatum about returning his possessions.

"You said, 'I want my stuff back or you'll never see your son again'," Justice Jago said.

"You were prepared to utter emotional threats to the complainant's father.

" Your conduct was disgraceful. "

A short time later, Brady Ludbey freed the boy from the container, returned his phone and told him to go home.

The boy was taken to hospital with minor physical injuries, but Justice Jago said she had no doubt the psychological harm was "significant" and that he would have been "deeply traumatised".

Justice Jago told the court that Ludbey had not shown remorse. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Judge lashes man for 'lack of insight'

At the outset of proceedings, defence lawyer Greg Richardson said it was his "privilege" to provide the court with 49 separate character references from people who supported Ludbey.

Justice Jago, however, said she found it "difficult to reconcile" the letters praising Ludbey's character with his "egregious behaviour".

She said that generally, people who are described as pillars of their community "do not behave in this way", although his character was supported by the fact he had not committed similar crimes before or since the attack.

However, she said Ludbey had not shown remorse and had demonstrated "a serious lack of insight into the gravity" of his crimes.

"This was premeditated violence carried out for vindictive reasons," the judge said.

She sentenced Ludbey to 14 months' jail, of which 10 months were suspended for two years.

In court, Ludbey was supported by more than a dozen people, several of whom became emotional when he was jailed.

World.title: 'Dumbest thing he's ever done': Canberra detective jailed for perjury
World.content:
A senior Australian Federal Police (AFP) detective who admitted to lying under oath about evidence seized during a criminal investigation will spend four months behind bars.

Trent Madders, 52, had pleaded guilty to a count of perjury, in that he knowingly made false statements in legal proceedings in August 2020.

In handing down his sentence in the ACT Supreme Court, Justice David Mossop said Madders's conduct reflected a "tragic misjudgement".

"The perjury was career destroying … and much more serious than the conduct it was trying to hide," Justice Mossop said.

He said Madders undermined the "proper administration of justice" and had an impact on the perception of police being honest and reliable.

Case centres around evidence seized

Madders was the officer in charge of the 2019 investigation into identical twin brothers Joshua, who was also an AFP officer, and Kenan Tiffen, who were accused of secretly filming female tenants at a Canberra property they owned.

During the investigation, police seized a mobile phone and laptop which were required to be examined within 30 days unless an extension was granted.

Madders did not seek an extension and was later told by AFP digital forensics staff that the devices had not been examined within the required time-frame.

Madders admitted his offending was the "dumbest thing he's ever done". (Supplied)

But when the admissibility of the evidence was challenged in the ACT Magistrates Court in 2020, Madders gave sworn evidence that he had been assured the devices had been examined in time.

He maintained that account under cross-examination despite being confronted with emails showing otherwise, and has since admitted those statements were knowingly false.

The Tiffen brothers were initially found guilty in 2022, but successfully appealed their convictions after evidence obtained from the laptop was ruled unlawful.

The case was sent back to the ACT Magistrates Court and the brothers were found guilty again in September 2025 of attempting to capture indecent visual data.

Lies were 'deliberately told': prosecution

Prosecutor Keegan Lee argued Madders's lies were "deliberately told, repeated and maintained".

"This is an offence that strikes at the heart of the administration of justice," he told the court.

" This is not a minor or momentary lapse of judgement. "

Defence barrister Beth Morrisroe said Madders admitted his offending was the "dumbest thing he has ever done".

"He is remorseful, he has demonstrated insight … he has taken accountability," she said.

She described Madders as an "overworked" officer who was experiencing significant stress, pressure and fatigue.

The judge described Madders's offending as a "tragic misjudgement". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Due to his time in the police force in the ACT, the court heard it was likely he would need to be transferred to a "far away" New South Wales correctional facility if a jail sentence was imposed.

But Ms Morrisroe argued he would be exposed to a "heightened level of risk" in any prison due to the national media attention he received through his involvement in investigating Brittany Higgins's rape allegation.

Justice Mossop sentenced him to almost a year in prison, to be suspended after four months, after which he will be subject to a good behaviour order.

Madders has been suspended from duty with the AFP since he was charged in 2024.

The AFP has been contacted for comment.

World.title: As bird flu ravages stocks, Kangaroo Island is 'sick of bloody disasters'
World.content:
Kangaroo Island locals on the frontline against bird flu are fearful of further devastation, with the mayor saying he is "sick of bloody disasters".

It was yesterday revealed that three mass bird deaths believed to be linked to H5N1 and involving more than 1,000 crested terns had occurred on remote SA islands — including two off KI.

A suspected case involving a little penguin found on D'Estrees Bay on the island's southern coastline is also being investigated.

"It was distressing and it really gets us worried over here about where this is all going — terribly distressing for the community," Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly said of the mass mortalities.

" We're providing facilities for dead birds to go into at our waste depot. The department is sending over eco bins for the birds to decompose in, so we're doing what we can. "

Penguins at Penneshaw on Kangaroo Island, where the current population is estimated to be about 200. (Supplied: Penneshaw Penguin Centre)

The SA government has said it is now considering a potential vaccination program for certain species, including penguins.

Penneshaw Penguin Centre tour operator Renee Daniell said it had been "heartbreaking to hear" of the mass mortality events, which occurred on North Page and South Page off KI and Troubridge Island off Yorke Peninsula.

She said the local penguin population had rebounded in recent years after other challenges, but the spread of H5N1 was making her nervous.

"We've been following it for about a month now but it sort of got a lot more real yesterday with how hard it could hit," she said.

Renee Daniell says the Penneshaw penguin population is currently strong, but she is monitoring for changes. (ABC News)

"We monitor a colony that's got about 100 penguins in the area that we monitor — the whole Penneshaw population's about 200 penguins at the moment.

" These guys have over doubled their numbers in the last four years and we're seeing really consistent numbers with breeding season so it'll be devastating if we start seeing massive losses to the colony. "

Ms Daniell's business is on the north coast of the island, and she said it was popular with tourists "from all around the world coming to see the penguins".

"[We] don't like waking up at five o'clock in the morning worried about what's going to happen on the day or going out for a walk every morning to go and see if I can find a dead penguin — it's not something we enjoy doing," she said.

Dozens of dead birds on Baudin Rocks, an island south of Robe, were recorded earlier this year. (Supplied: SA Government)

Environment Minister Emily Bourke said the penguin found at D'Estrees Bay was "in the process of being tested" for H5N1.

She said the number of cases at an earlier mass mortality site — Baudin Rocks — was now suspected to have exceeded 500.

Push for penguin vaccination

Mr Pengilly said the island had been lashed in recent years by a succession of calamities, and that little penguins had "taken a hammering" during the algal bloom.

"I'm sick of bloody disasters," he said with a wry smile.

"We had the fires six years ago where half the island was burnt out, then we had COVID, then we had algal bloom, now we've got bird flu.

"We lost thousands of animals, tens of thousands of birds in the fires — they've recovered.

"Last year with the algal bloom we had our fish stocks decimated — they're recovering quite quickly so we hope at the end of this our bird life recovers."

Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly says the island has been hit with multiple disasters in recent years. (ABC News)

Ms Daniell said she had sought biosecurity advice and had organised meetings for Monday with the primary industries and environment departments.

"We've been told to look out for signs of things like [birds] being lethargic or not moving properly, which is concerning," she said.

"Hopefully we look at even the opportunity of vaccinating the colony, given that we are a monitored colony and we are going through breeding season at the moment.

"If it's something that could potentially protect these little penguins, I ultimately am — I suppose — pro."

Little penguin researcher Stephen Hedges says so far the birds on Granite Island haven't been affected. (ABC News: Caroline Horn)

About 65 kilometres away, as the crows flies, Granite Island off Victor Harbor is home to another population of little penguins, and local volunteer Stephen Hedges is bracing for bird flu's impact.

"Often it's the first wave that's going to be really tough," he said.

"Bird flu comes back each year, like our flu — but the more tolerance they can develop, the better."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said vaccination was currently being considered, but that decisions would be made based on various factors, and that there would need to be a "regulatory and approval process to make sure it's safe".

The SA government says it is now considering vaccination, with decisions to be made based on various factors. (ABC News: Caroline Horn)

"We have already commenced the process in conjunction with Cleland [Wildlife Park] but also the Adelaide Zoo," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"The vaccine is still early in its development.

"To be able to administer the vaccine we have to be able to catch the bird and then we have to be able to do it twice.

"For birds of flight that is obviously difficult. For flightless birds, that task is a little bit easier, provided that they are a species that return to their burrows."

World.title: Top lawyer calls out 'absurd criticism' of Big Build royal commission
World.content:
The anti-corruption barrister who estimated $15 billion in taxpayer funding was wasted on Victoria's Big Build has accused the opposition of making "absurd" criticisms of Premier Ben Carroll's royal commission, which he said was "excellently" designed.

Mr Carroll released the terms of reference for a royal commission into the integrity of major projects in Victoria yesterday. His predecessor, Jacinta Allan, had refused to heed calls for such an inquiry and was dogged for years by alleged wrongdoing and corruption on government construction sites.

The terms specifically cover the executive level of government. But Shadow Attorney-General James Newbury claimed without evidence that Ms Allan and former premier Daniel Andrews would not be hauled before the commission.

"The government has explicitly ruled out in the terms of reference certain behaviour of the CFMEU," Mr Newbury also claimed in an interview with ABC Melbourne radio yesterday.

Geoffrey Watson, SC, said the terms of reference were "really excellently done".

"I think they're very well designed, quite targeted, and sufficiently specific," he said.

Geoffrey Watson has long been an outspoken advocate for a royal commission into Victoria's construction industry. (Supplied)

Mr Watson said it was unheard of to dictate witnesses for a royal commission. Doing so would affect its independence, he said, and ruling some people in could allow other potential witnesses to claim they are out of the scope of the investigation.

"This is an absurd criticism, frankly," Mr Watson told the ABC today.

"I think it's a mistake for people to go out and start undermining confidence in the commission before it starts. After all, this is a process through which we're hoping the confidence in government will be rebuilt. Now, why criticise it at this time? I do not know why, and I might make another point: the criticism is incorrect."

Mr Carroll rejected the suggestion Ms Allan or Mr Andrews would not be called, having confirmed that ministers and former premiers would be fair game under the terms.

"Anyone and everyone can be called. These are the most comprehensive, broadest terms possible," Mr Carroll told reporters today.

"We're going to make sure that we leave no stone unturned."

The terms of reference cover the conduct of the CFMEU, construction companies, labour hire firms and criminal actors on Victoria's major projects. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

Integrity bodies and business leaders broadly welcomed the terms of reference this week.

A timeline for hearings and a witness list are yet to be established. These decisions are up to the commissioner, former South Australian Supreme Court chief justice Christopher Kourakis, who has a $50 million budget and will report back within 12 months.

Mr Watson's estimation that $15 billion had been lost on Victoria's program of major projects had cut through to the public, set off a spat with Ms Allan, and infected the electorate's perception of core Labor government deliverables, like the Metro Tunnel and North East Link.

"The point of me putting an estimate on it was to do just that: put an estimate on it, because I was calling for a royal commission," Mr Watson said.

"I'm confident that this royal commission will do a great job."

Jacinta Allan announced she would not contest the 2026 Victorian election on August 14 at a press conference in Bendigo. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Mr Newbury further claimed the premier said he did not want to get to the bottom of the $15 billion figure. The terms ask the commission to determine the impact of wrongdoing on construction costs of the Big Build and to identify means of recouping that.

He questioned whether $50 million would be enough for the commission to do its job.

The terms have a broad focus on the causes, contributing factors and any preconditions that allowed wrongdoing.

Lawful, legitimate and appropriate actions under industrial rules and occupational health and safety laws will be exempted, but the terms go to "the misuse or abuse" of these regulations.

World.title: Community pantry dobbed in to council for being on public kerbside
World.content:
A neighbourhood pantry that provides free food to struggling families has been dobbed in to the Brisbane City Council for being on a public kerbside.

The Everton Park Community Pantry receives produce from grocers, bakeries, and farms — food that otherwise would have ended up in landfill.

Nelika McDonald and her husband James Paterson set up the pantry in 2024 outside their home on South Pine Road.

Brisbane City Council told 612 ABC it received four complaints from residents about "safety concerns" and restricted footpath access.

Ms McDonald said she received a visit from a council officer on Wednesday, telling her she was illegally "depositing articles" on council land.

The items include a cabinet of canned food, a table, a donation bin, and a shelter, which are permanently kept on the kerbside.

The community pantry is stocked twice per day. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Ms McDonald said the volunteers made sure to keep the footpath itself clear so that pedestrians could walk through.

She said she was shocked to learn that she had been reported to the council.

"We were pretty upset about that because we've been operating for two years now and we don't see the harm in what we're doing," Ms McDonald said.

"The pantry is for people in need, which there's a lot of at the moment with the cost of living crisis."

Homeless and hungry

Cath Mulcahy says the pantry kept her fed after she lost everything in 2024. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Cath Mulcahy said she started using the pantry two years ago, after becoming homeless and at the age of 66.

The now 68-year-old said she had been living in her car, and frequently could not afford to eat.

"I stumbled on this place one Sunday, and I opened the door and got a can of tuna and a can of beans, and I had lunch," she said.

"Otherwise I would not have had anything to eat.

" I rely heavily on the goodwill of what comes through here. "

Ms Mulcahy said she had made many friendships with the people who used the community pantry, many of whom were also homeless.

She said, increasingly, many of them were older women like herself.

A Brisbane City Council spokesperson said they were in ongoing discussions with Everton Park Community Pantry.

"We recognise the important support the Everton Park Community Pantry and its volunteers provide to people in the local community, and we want to see that valuable work continue," the spokesperson said.

"Our priority is keeping everyone safe, including the volunteers, people accessing the pantry, pedestrians and other road users.

"We are committed to working constructively with the Everton Park Community Pantry to find a practical way forward that supports its important work while addressing the safety concerns that have been raised."

World.title: Mobile phones are 'Trojan horses' for germs. Here's how to clean them
World.content:
I've never cleaned my mobile phone, but after chatting with experts for this story, it was the first thing I did.

It turns out mobile phones are "Trojan horses" for carrying germs. That's according to Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular biology and genomics at Bond University and Murdoch University.

He found more than 17,000 micro-organisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, living on 95 mobile phones he studied.

And with 80 per cent of people surveyed by Dr Tajouri admitting to using their phone in a public toilet, we can start to understand how they get there.

"Mobile phones behave like biological magnets," he says, adding their warm and moist conditions act like "five-star hotel accommodation for microorganisms".

If you're understandably grossed out, keep reading to find out the best way to clean your phone, and how often you need to be doing it.

What lives on our phone and is it harmful?

In the 95 phones Dr Tajouri and his team analysed, they also found super bugs (germs that are very hard to treat), antibiotic resistant genes, and virulence factor genes (these increase a pathogen's ability to cause disease).

He says micro-organisms thrive on phones because they are high-touch surfaces that deliver the right "breeding ground" conditions.

"We load them with all sorts of microbes through our fingers … and when we talk into them, we drop little droplets of saliva.

" Moisture with heat is the perfect condition for multiplication. "

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

We transfer these germs back to our faces, Dr Tajouri says, by touching our lips, eyes and nose on average 25 times in an hour.

"Eighty per cent of common infections are associated with hands. Mobile phones negate handwashing."

Immunocompromised people are most at risk of illness from their phones, Dr Tajouri says.

"That includes infants, the elderly, and of course people with chronic disease like diabetes."

Meena Jha, head of technology at Central Queensland University, says while having germs on your phone doesn't "automatically make you sick", we do need to be practising good hand and surface hygiene.

"I wouldn't describe the phone as inherently dangerous. But it's about recognising it's a frequently touched surface that can catch microbes.

"We should be cleaning them, and we often forget."

Who is cleaning their phone anyway?

Research shows 80 per cent of people admit to using mobile phones in public toilets. (Pexels: Miriam Alonso)

Not me (until recently), but I'm in good company.

According to Dr Tajouri's research, most participants never or rarely clean their devices.

For example, a survey he conducted with hospital staff in Queensland found 52 per cent admitted to using their mobile phones in the toilet, and 57 per cent said they never cleaned them.

How to clean your phone without damaging it

Before cleaning your phone, you need to unplug it (if it's being charged) and remove any protective cases and accessories, explains Dr Jha.

"For most modern phones, a soft microfibre cloth is the safest starting point," she says.

If you want to disinfect it, Dr Jha recommends no higher than 70 per cent isopropyl alcohol wipes, which is in line with most guidelines backed by major manufacturers.

"Use it gently, and the most important thing is to not spray anything directly onto the phone."

She says any cloths or wipes should be damp, not dripping wet, as you want to keep moisture away from charging ports and speakers.

For those areas, Dr Jha says you can use a soft, dry brush.

How dirty are public toilet seats? Public toilets are a "microbial soup" and there are things you should be doing to protect yourself — including not taking out your mobile phone and never hovering over the seat.

And avoid any strong cleaning products.

"Anything that can be harmful for your kitchen top — you should not be using that," Dr Jha says.

For example, she says vinegar, bleach and hydrogen peroxide are too aggressive for a smartphone's "oleophobic layer".

"That layer resists fingerprints and smudges. Harsh chemicals and excessive scrubbing will gradually strip this coating and reduce touch responsiveness."

Dr Jha recommends cleaning your phone once a week "but context matters".

If you are regularly taking your phone into a hospital setting, for example, you may like to clean more frequently.

Dr Jha warns against being "obsessive" about cleaning as it may damage the device.

Reducing germ risk and spread

Dr Tajouri is particularly passionate about people not using their phones in toilets to help reduce risk.

He says public toilets are often not cleaned frequently or well, "and we touch a lot of contaminated areas: faucets, flush button, doorknobs, toilet seat. Then we touch our phone."

"And when you flush, there is a plume effect."

Dr Tajouri says droplets from the toilet bowl can contain bacteria and viruses and travel up to 2 metres.

If you are taking your phone into the toilet, he says to close the lid before flushing and avoid using the hand dryer, which also spreads germs around.

World.title: Man, 47, charged with threatening to kill Pauline Hanson
World.content:
A Perth man has appeared in court accused of threatening to kill One Nation leader Pauline Hanson.

Anton Raymond Illich, 47, is accused of making three Facebook posts, including on a One Nation members and supporters page.

In one of the posts, Mr Illich said he would "hunt her down and kill her", a Perth court has heard.

The 47-year-old was charged in July with two counts of using a carriage service to make a threat, but it was only revealed today in court Ms Hanson was the subject of the threats.

Mr Illich, who was representing himself, admitted it was "stupid, crazy" and told the court he did it because he wanted to shut down his Facebook account.

He said he had no intent and he was "never a direct threat".

Mr Illich indicated he wanted to plead guilty, but the court heard that the matter is likely to go to a higher court.

The magistrate ordered that he cannot contact Ms Hanson.

The Australian Federal Police said in July it had started an investigation after receiving notification of an alleged online threat to kill a federal parliamentarian.

The identities of the accused and the parliamentarian were not revealed at the time.

The maximum penalty for the offence is ten years in prison.

Mr Illich, who's on bail, is scheduled to appear in the magistrates court again in October.

Ms Hanson travelled to Western Australia last month for a business breakfast, and also held a fundraiser at a pub in Midland in June, which saw dozens of protesters line the surrounding streets.

World.title: Fair Work warning as court action looms over berry pickers' pay
World.content:
Australia's Fair Work Ombudsman has issued a stark warning to labour-hire firms and farms that are underpaying workers in the Coffs Harbour region: "We are coming for you."

The message came as Fair Work filed a case in the Federal Court against a labour-hire company accused of underpaying two workers about $20,000.

Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said court action had been taken against three labour-hire companies so far this year, two of which were operating on the Coffs Coast.

"If you are underpaying workers in the Coffs Harbour region … then you should be on notice and checking your own supply chain to make sure it is compliant with the Fair Work Act," she said.

" Because we are coming for you. "

Fair Work has alleged Four Seasons Workforce Pty Ltd was paying workers on a piecework basis, according to how much they picked.

It has accused the company of not complying with the Pieceworker Guaranteed Minimum Rate, which guarantees workers are paid no less than the minimum hourly rate for casual fruit pickers under the Horticulture Industry Award 2020.

Anna Booth says court action has been filed against three companies so far this year. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Earlier this month, a report into modern slavery raised serious concerns about labour-hire firms operating on the Coffs and Mid North coasts, with some workers reporting they were earning less than $7 an hour and were living in overcrowded, squalid accommodation.

The ombudsman took action against Four Seasons Workforce, and the company's sole director, Pik Yok Chey, after Fair Work received complaints from two workers, a Chinese national and a Japanese national.

The pair were both in Australia on working holiday visas, and were both allegedly underpaid at different intervals between July 2023 and October 2024.

Four Seasons Workforce Pty Ltd could face penalties of up to $99,000 per offence and Ms Chey could face penalties of up to $19,800 per offence if the allegations are proven in the Federal Court.

The Fair Work Ombudsman has alleged the company also failed to act on compliance notices within the required time frame.

Ms Booth said Fair Work was seeing underpayments across the horticultural industry.

"We see them in the labour-hire industry predominantly," she said.

"Many growers engage labour-hire companies to supply labour and … this region [Coffs Harbour] is one of our top trouble spot regions that we have identified through our investigations."

Kun Du was working on a blueberry farm in the Coffs Harbour region from June and October 2024. ( Supplied: Fair Work Ombudsman)

'I had to borrow money'

When Chinese national Kun Du was working on a blueberry farm on the Coffs Coast, she was allegedly paid so little that she could not afford groceries.

"At times, I had to borrow money from the supervisor on site," Ms Du said in a statement provided by Fair Work.

When she took her case to Fair Work, Four Seasons Workforce allegedly paid her $5,000.

In a statement, Fair Work said the company also allegedly repaid $14,065 to a Japanese national after the ombudsman started legal action.

"When I saw the money, it felt like justice had been served," Ms Du said.

The Fair Work Ombudsman is taking a labour-hire company to court after it allegedly underpaid workers. (ABC Landline)

Ms Booth said workers who were on temporary visas were "particularly vulnerable".

"They are often unaware of Australian terms and conditions, they're sometimes nervous about coming to the regulator," she said.

"We do want visa holders to know they have the same rights as any Australian worker, that they can obtain our support and their visa will be protected."

The ABC was unable to contact Four Seasons Workforce for a response.

The case is set to be mentioned in the Federal Court on October 20.

World.title: Bad code turned bushwalker search into an even sadder tragedy
World.content:
NationalNSWMissing person Editorial Bad code turned bushwalker search into an even sadder tragedy The Herald's View Editorial August 21, 2026 — 4:02pm

August 21, 2026 — 4:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lost in the bush has long haunted Australia. The bush can be alien, and the experience is reflected in the many works – poems, books and films – about our lost children. Sometimes they never came back. Sometimes they were found. But not this time. NSW Police unwittingly compounded the tragedy by allowing word to get out that 18-year-old Lily Hooper, a hiker missing for eight days in bushland south-west of Sydney, had been found alive, only to confirm some 20 minutes later that she had died. Friends, family and loved ones of Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper have been grieving her loss after initially hearing she had been found alive. Hooper left home on August 12 for a hike in Nattai National Park. She did not return. Almost 1000 people joined the search, including some 100 Australian Defence Force personnel, 280 NSW SES volunteers, Rural Fire Service firefighters and specialist police crews.



Shortly before 11.30 on Thursday, a search team radioed the operator. She’d been found. A police officer at the search base, on the edge of the Nattai National Park, told Hooper’s parents, Jim and Kirrily Hooper, that their daughter was alive; Police Minister Yasmin Catley passed on the information to Premier Chris Minns, who interrupted budget estimates to announce the hiker was alive. But then, the horrifying update came; the news had been wrong. She was dead. A multi-agency investigation has now been launched to examine the cluster of failures. The Herald’s Riley Walter reported the miscommunication may have been sparked by a radio code believed to be used by SES searchers to report that a body has been found, in which they refer to full, half or empty water bottles to signal whether a person is alive, in the event family members may be monitoring the radio. A half bottle of water is believed to indicate a person’s condition is unclear. In the immediate aftermath, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon shouldered the blame, apologising to the Hooper family and Minns. “The miscommunication obviously was born out of elation that Lily had been found, and her condition at that time was such that searchers were relieved, and certainly those at the command post relayed,” he said. “Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously, we know now an impact on her family.” But other leaders were nowhere to be seen.



Emergency Services Minister Jihad Dib and NSW SES commissioner Mike Wassing waited until the following morning to appear. Wassing said: “It’s quite common that during search and rescue operations, police will set a code for the search and rescue operators to use with respect to if they find the missing person. In this case, there was a code that was applied. We’re working currently with police with respect to any of the misinformation associated with that code or any subsequent further information or communication.” Wassing also said authorities were not looking at blame but that they simply wished to identify how the code had been either mistaken or misheard. But the Hooper search imbroglio has exposed several flaws in communication processes that demand an urgent review of protocols. It’s the job of the professionals in the search, in this case the NSW Police and paid leaders of the SES to ensure volunteers, an essential arm of rescue work in our state, are properly briefed. The tragedy visited on the Hooper family by confusion over bad code cannot be repeated. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ASX Runners of the Week: Genesis, Triton, Pure One & DXN
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: Genesis, Triton, Pure One & DXN Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd August 21, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The gold bugs are definitely back and beaming this week. After months of being whacked by months of war-induced inflationary pressures leading to a resilient US dollar, the shiny yellow metal came roaring back to life as cracks began appearing in the American economy. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Genesis Resource. July’s non-farm payrolls (non-seasonal jobs) unexpectedly went backwards in reporting this week, shedding 23,000 jobs and reinforcing the view that the world’s largest economy may finally be cooling. Traders immediately began scaling back expectations of further rate hikes, while bond markets staged an unexpected rally after the US Treasury quietly doubled its planned buybacks of long-dated debt in an attempt to steady the bond market.



The Government printing more money to add to the already-groaning weight of more than US$40 trillion (A$61 trillion) in national debt is never a good sign of prosperity. The result was a familiar one. The US dollar softened to a runny egg and gold exploded higher, surging to more than six per cent to US$4550 (A$6910). Copper, meanwhile, refused to give an inch, holding firm near US$6.50 (A$9.95) per pound as the market struggles amid chronic supply shortages, remaining a powerful long-term red metal driver. Back home, Australia’s own inflation architects were quietly celebrating a milestone of their own. Federal debt has now blown through the trillion-dollar mark, leaving taxpayers with the privilege of funding record government spending while somehow managing higher taxes, higher electricity prices and a cost-of-living crisis that seemingly adds more brainwash initiatives by the second. An unexpected, good news story of the week came in the final reprieve for the ASX’s healthcare index, which was up a staggering 14 per cent in just one week. Former market darling and once Australia’s largest listed company, CSL, has had a ripping week after the healthcare giant spent the past year being treated like a biotech penny dreadful, shedding almost $90 billion in value from its highs. Investors finally decided enough was enough. The stock exploded nearly 18 per cent in a single session after management delivered better-than-expected FY26 numbers and forecasts for the year to come.



The resources sector also continued to remind everyone where Australia’s real economic engine sits BHP surged almost seven per cent as copper held its ground as the market’s metal of choice, while New Zealand’s biggest precious metals producer, OceanaGold, lobbed a hefty $776 million bid for Ausgold’s Katanning gold project in Western Australia. It seems OceanaGold, unable to expand its considerable resource base in NZ thanks to the government’s insistence on ignoring its own mineral wealth, has decided it’s time to expand into WA. The message is clear: quality ounces are making the big players move and they’re no longer waiting for developers to build the mines themselves. The Bulls N’ Bears Runners cavalcade this week perfectly mirrored the renewed gold sentiment, with the precious metal once again stamping its authority on the list. Pay-outs and payloads were the themes of the week for the minors, with a plucky gas explorer also making a late charge after plunging a well into one of Queensland’s most prolific gas basins. GENESIS RESOURCES LTD (ASX: GES) Up 500% (0.5c – 3c)



The Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is Genesis Resources, which took off in spectacular fashion this week after returning rock chip grades of up to 28.8 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from reconnaissance sampling at its Arltunga copper-gold project in the Northern Territory. Now, high-grade gold samples from surface are always going to get the market’s attention, but one struggles to recall too many occasions where a handful of rock chips have ignited a 500 per cent share price rally. Genesis rocketed to a high of 3c this week – its highest point in almost a decade. With gold back in favour and the company’s tightly held share register acting as an amplifier for every buy order, it was the perfect storm for this feisty junior to claim the top spot. The company collected 53 reconnaissance samples from previously undrilled areas across its exploration licence 100 kilometres northeast of Alice Springs, with standout results coming from the newly identified WP-10 prospect, where separate samples returned impressive assays of 11.25g/t and 10.47g/t gold. Along trend at Genesis’ Star Creek prospect, samples also delivered grades at an impressive 13.71g/t and 6.41g/t gold from around historical workings that include old trenches and a 10-metre-deep shaft, all crying out to be tested at depth. Even the company’s Jenkins Mine, which returned modest surface grades of up to 0.88g/t gold, comes with a tantalising backstory. Historical records from the Northern Territory Geological Survey suggest the mine once operated at an average head grade of a hefty 34.7g/t gold, which is yet to be tested by modern exploration.



With a clutch of high-grade targets now in hand, Genesis plans to drill-test WP-10, Star Creek, Chinaman’s Workings and Jenkins during the 2027 field season. The company also added a tasty kicker, collecting 10 rock-chip samples from previously untested areas on its Alice Springs tenement before unseasonal rain brought the field program to an early end. One of those samples returned 1.2 per cent copper roughly 300 metres northeast of the nearest drill hole at the Diana 2 prospect, with follow-up fieldwork now planned. Gold and copper remain two of the hottest commodities in town, and Genesis appears to have a solid footing in both. The market has already cast its vote on the surface results. Now comes the real test – whether those flashy grades can survive the journey from a rock on the surface to a drill core at depth. TRITON MINERALS LTD (ASX: TON) Up 100% (0.25c – 0.5c) Stealing second place this week is Triton Minerals, whose shares doubled after the company finally drew a line under a long-running dispute and secured a pathway to complete the sale of a 70 per cent stake in its Mozambique graphite assets.



A new deed of settlement has now resolved the legal proceedings that stemmed from its partner, NQM Gold 2 Pty Ltd, missing staged payments under the original agreement, which was worth about $17 million. Under the latest deal, the transaction will complete on August 21, with Triton set to receive the remaining $5.5 million held in trust. NQM will take ownership of 70 per cent of the assets, while Triton will retain a substantial 30 per cent stake in the joint venture. Accordingly, court proceedings will now be discontinued. The market’s excitement is understandable given the sheer scale of the graphite assets involved. Triton’s flagship Ancuabe project hosts a JORC mineral resource of 46 million tonnes grading 6.6 per cent total graphitic carbon for 3.04 million tonnes of contained graphite. A definitive feasibility study has already outlined a production profile of 60,000 tonnes of graphite concentrate per year over a mine life stretching almost three decades, involving a valuable mix of large and jumbo graphite flakes. The bigger prize, however, may well be the Cobra Plains deposit.Hosting a massive inferred resource of 103 million tonnes grading 5.2 per cent total graphitic carbon for a staggering 5.7 million tonnes of contained graphite, the asset also benefits from sitting within a 25-year mining concession. Combined, the Mozambique assets contain almost 9 million tonnes of graphite resources, making them among the biggest undeveloped graphite inventories on the ASX. With environmental approvals, mining concessions and development studies already in place, the market appears to be betting that this settlement finally clears the path for the projects to move from courtroom battles to mine development.



With legal clarification, a booming graphite market and $5.5 million in cash on its way, Triton’s story looks like it can finally get back on track. A Silver City rig drilling Pure One’s Venus-2H well in the prolific Surat Basin, in Queensland. PURE ONE CORP LTD (ASX: P1E) Up 91% (3.3c – 6.3c) We love a late runner at Bulls N’ Bears, and junior energy hopeful Pure One Corp has made a late dash for the final podium spot on Friday.



The company announced strong gas shows at its Venus-2H horizontal appraisal well in Queensland’s Surat Basin, with total gas readings hitting up to 25.4 per cent as drilling continues towards its intersection with the Venus-1 wellbore. Project Venus is a first-rate asset because it sits in the heart of Queensland’s premier Walloon Fairway, the most proven and productive coal-seam gas province in the state. This area has already seen more than 10,000 wells drilled and supplies the bulk of the gas that feeds the LNG export facilities at Gladstone. The permit is surrounded by major operators such as Origin, Apollo, Arrow, QGC and Santos, meaning the geology is well understood, the infrastructure is dense and commercial pathways are already established. The current Venus-2 well is an appraisal, commercial-style horizontal well designed to prove gas deliverability. It has been drilled vertically to about 420m, before turning horizontal for approximately 1km. It will then intersect the existing Venus-1 well for dewatering, followed by flow testing. Every previous well on the block has already produced gas to surface, giving management high confidence. The implications for Pure One are compelling. The junior explorer retains a controlling 69.4 per cent stake in Eastern Gas Corporation, the listed vehicle that now holds and funds the project. A successful commercial flow test would therefore deliver a material uplift in value directly to Pure One’s balance sheet and share price, without the company having to fund the full development itself. New domestic and exportable gas supply is definitely back from the doldrums in Australia and proving a commercial resource in this location could rapidly re-rate Pure One.



The discovery could transform from a pure junior explorer into a company with a de-risked, infrastructure-adjacent gas asset - a powerful catalyst sitting comfortably alongside its additional technology, which is focused on an EV-vehicle launch planned for next month. The company recently rebranded from Pure Hydrogen to Pure One to reflect its expansion into battery-electric and multi-technology clean mobility solutions. The focus is on capital-light, partner-manufactured vehicles using proven components, targeting commercial and government fleets where battery-swap technology is especially attractive. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… DXN Limited. DXN LIMITED (ASX: DXN) Up 35% (21.5c – 29c)



Rounding out our runners list is Bulls N’ Bears regular DXN Limited. While its 35 per cent gain for the week was modest compared to the others, the broader story for this data centre specialist is astounding. The company announced that it had been awarded a contract by Australia Pacific Airports, the operator of Melbourne Airport. Under the agreement, DXN will design, manufacture, deliver, install and commission a prefabricated Edge Data Centre facility, with the contract valued at approximately $4.1 million. This comes on the heels of an $8.8 million deal inked recently with a US Neo-Cloud operator, which could be worth up to US$200 million (A$280M) in future orders. DXN’s point of difference in the data-centre world lies in its speed-to-deployment, modular scalability and direct liquid cooling expertise. Subject to successful delivery, the Melbourne Airport operator has indicated its intent to progress to a substantially larger campus program, representing a potential revenue opportunity for DXN well in excess of US$200 million for the existing site in the next one to two years. Airports operate a dense mix of latency-sensitive, safety-critical systems that increasingly require compute and network capacity to be physically located near the operations they serve, rather than being housed in a distant central facility. The award builds on DXN’s track record of delivering prefabricated critical infrastructure for government, telecommunications and blue-chip enterprise customers across the Asia Pacific. With its share price now up nearly 1300 per cent since its lows in May, DXN is once again raising its hand to be in contention for Runners of the Year 2026 glory when it is all said and done. World.title: Fourth Sydney Airport safety incident under investigation in as many weeks
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Fourth Sydney Airport safety incident under investigation in as many weeks Chris Zappone Updated August 21, 2026 — 3:45pm ,first published 11:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Investigators are examining how two Qantas flights at Sydney Airport were given clearance to take the same route on a taxiway on Tuesday. The incident is the fourth in the past four weeks at the airport, where shortages of air traffic controllers in its tower are being blamed for frequent delays. A Qantas 737 at Sydney Airport in a file photo. Wolter Peeters The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said a Qantas 737 arriving from the Gold Coast was heading west on the ground and had clearance to turn right. At the same time, a Qantas Airbus A321 preparing to depart for Melbourne also had clearance to turn, which would have put it in the other plane’s path.



“As the Airbus approached ... the crew observed the Boeing approaching from the left and stopped the aircraft,” the bureau said. Related Article Aviation Sydney Airport has had three close calls in as many weeks. The first big problem is clear Scrutiny over the operations of air traffic controllers has increased in the past month, following a series of incidents primarily at Sydney Airport. The safety bureau is also investigating a runway incursion and a rejected take-off of Virgin Australia flight VA555 from Sydney to Perth and Qantas flight QF728 from Sydney to Ayers Rock Airport on August 9. On the same day, a Jetstar A320 almost collided with a Qatar Airways Boeing 777. That incident was initially described as a near collision, although the bureau later called it a “proximity event”.



On the latest investigation, on August 18, the bureau said: “The evidence collection phase of the investigation will involve interviewing involved air traffic controllers and flight crew, retrieving and reviewing available recorded data, and the collection of other relevant information.” The bureau said in a statement it would look at the instructions given to flight crews and whether there were common factors with the spate of other incidents at Sydney Airport. There was no immediate risk of collision, it said, as the Qantas A321 aircraft was braking normally before coming to a stop. The bureau classified the event as a safety “incident” rather than a “serious incident”. It will conduct an investigation “to understand the potential conflicting instructions to the flight crews and whether there are any contributing factors common across the other Sydney Airport incidents currently under investigation”. A Qantas spokesperson said: “Our aircraft was cleared to proceed following instructions from air traffic control and we will support the ATSB in the investigation.”



Airservices Australia, the government-owned body in charge of air traffic control, said it reported the August 18 incident to the bureau as “involving a potential traffic conflict between two Qantas aircraft taxiing on the ground using the taxiway system”. The smooth operation of Sydney Airport’s tower has been the source of concern from the airline industry, which has complained about regular delays at the major airport. iStock Airservices described the report as part of its safety management system process. ”As with all reported occurrences, we will provide the bureau with all relevant information and act on any findings arising from its investigation,” an Airservices spokesperson said. “The recent ground traffic incidents currently under investigation by the bureau involve a range of circumstances, and each incident is being investigated on its individual facts.



Related Article Editorial

Airports We’re used to airport queues and delays, but safety is not negotiable The Herald's View Editorial “Airservices will continue to review operational events and take any action required to maintain safe operations.” The smooth operation of Sydney Airport’s tower has been the source of concern from the airline industry, which has complained about regular delays at the major airport. Some air traffic controllers have expressed concern over increased workload related to the opening of Western Sydney International. On July 27, a QantasLink flight and a Qantas flight were involved in a near miss on the tarmac in Sydney.



The incidents have raised concern about the staffing at Sydney’s air traffic control tower, which is under increasing pressure. Airservices said that in 12 months to July 2025, the bureau had received more than 14,600 aviation notifications from across the industry. Airservices submits multiple reports to the ATSB daily “as part of regular operational procedure”. University of Sydney professor Rico Merkert said for many instances involving towing vehicles or activity on the taxiway, the impact of an incident potentially “wouldn’t be that large”. “But having said that, recently there have been at least a couple, where the impact would be actually quite significant.” Deploying more sensors helped decision-makers focus on keeping planes safe, Merkert said. “The closer you get to the gate, the more you can automate the decision-making.



“I think the lot can be done there to improve the current processes and make it easier for the decision maker.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: This footy president wants to stamp out inequality and misogyny in sport. She’s running for parliament
World.content:
Exclusive SportVictorian election This footy president wants to stamp out inequality and misogyny in sport. She’s running for parliament Hannah Kennelly August 21, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Natalie Korinfsky stood “up to the blokes” at her football club. Now the president of the Wedge-Tailed Eagles – formerly known as the Kyneton Women’s Football Club – is running for Victorian parliament at a time when poor behaviour in sport is in the national spotlight. The Animal Justice Party has announced Natalie Korinfsky as its candidate for the seat of Macedon in the state election. Joe Armao Korinfsky led a high-profile battle for the Kyneton women’s right to play after they defected from their previous club following claims over inequitable treatment and disrespectful conditions. She has announced her candidacy in the upcoming state election for the Animal Justice Party in the seat of Macedon, which is held for Labor by retiring health minister Mary-Anne Thomas.





Purcell, who has been a prominent voice on women’s rights and against sexism herself, said Korinfsky’s decision to stand for parliament could not be more important. “For Natalie and her team of incredible women to not only stand up to the blokes at their club - but also the boys club that is the AFL - is nothing short of inspiring,” she said. “These are exactly the type of people that we need to see elected to our halls of power. “That is why Natalie running for parliament matters. We need people with lived experience of these environments at the table when laws are made to ensure that women’s safety isn’t just a buzz word. “Women shouldn’t have to fight this hard just to be heard. But when they do, we need to make sure they are given a seat at the table.”



Korinfsky told this masthead she would draw on her experiences in combatting discrimination in grassroots sports, focusing on standing up for those whose voices are often overlooked. Like many others, she added, she felt disheartened by the major parties for the upcoming election in November and wanted to bring more compassion to politics. Kyneton Women’s football team, now known as the Wedge-Tailed Eagles. Joe Armao “It’s probably something I never imagined doing,” she said. “With the state of politics, I think sometimes you just have to do things that are a little bit scary to try and enact some change.” Korinfsky is a social worker with experience in youth mental health and disability support, and has recently worked for Omnia Community Health, running programs to keep young people in education. She also wants to improve the state of community sporting facilities in Macedon.



She will be running against Labor candidate Annette Death and former Macedon Ranges mayor Kate Kendall, who will represent the Liberals. While she did not comment specifically on the Swans, Korinfsky said it was important to see strong leadership from the AFL and other sports, to encourage systematic change. “We’re not seeing our big sporting organisations and our government really come down on gender-based violence and sexism, misogyny,” she said. “Then how do we expect our sporting clubs on the ground to really know what to do?” MP Georgie Purcell (left) and Natalie Korinfsk



Purcell said if re-elected to parliament, the Animal Justice Party wanted to establish a state parliamentary inquiry into equity and inclusion in sport, and hear from communities about their experiences in sport, “whether that be sexism, homophobia, transphobia or racism”. Purcell was a vocal supporter of the Wedge-Tailed Eagles during their search for a league to play in, after the breakaway team’s application to the Central Victorian league was initially blocked by their former league, Riddell. In February, this masthead revealed that the vice-president of the Riddell District Football Netball League, Andrew Power, had resigned following a series of questions from The Age to the league about vulgar comments Power had left on the women’s team’s Instagram page. Shortly after, the AFL announced Kyneton Women’s Football Club could play in the Central Victorian Football League this season after 12 months in limbo under their new name, the Wedge-Tailed Eagles. When Purcell extended her support, she said she heard from many women from other sporting clubs in similar predicaments.



“Obviously, the Wedgies really set a standard and were incredibly brave and put their faces to it. But the reality is, so many people are afraid to even speak out, and we need to provide that forum for people to do so safely and perhaps confidentially to address this really serious and systemic problem,” she said. World.title: This 26-year-old former car salesman just quietly became a European prince
World.content:
WorldEuropeBelgium This 26-year-old former car salesman just quietly became a European prince Lilia Sebouai August 21, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man has become a prince at the age of 26 after the brother of the king of Belgium finally recognised him as his own. Prince Laurent is the brother of King Philippe and has long been labelled the “cursed prince” of the Saxe-Coburg house. Clément Vandenkerckhove in Jaunuary. Alamy Stock Photo He has registered his paternity of Clément Vandenkerckhove with the civil registry. Vandenkerckhove was born to Iris Vandenkerckhove – better known as singer, actress and socialite Wendy Van Wanten – before Prince Laurent’s 2003 marriage to Princess Claire, with whom he shares three children.



While civil recognition makes the former car salesman a prince and gives him equal inheritance rights to Prince Laurent’s private estate alongside his half-siblings, the royal perks stop there. Owing to Belgium’s 2013 royal endowment reforms, public funding is strictly limited to the reigning monarch and the direct heir. He will not be given a state stipend or official duties, and has zero rights to the throne. Belgium’s Princess Claire and Prince Laurent during National Day celebrations in July. Getty Images Laurent met Iris Vandenkerckhove at a Paris fashion show in the mid-90s and began a high-profile relationship. When their son was born in August 2000, the Belgian press immediately speculated about his paternity.



The name Clément was widely read as a direct nod to Villa Clémentine, Prince Laurent’s official residence in Tervuren, a Flemish town just outside Brussels. Iris Vandenkerckhove also repeatedly hinted at hidden lovers in several of her pop ballads. Iris Vandenkerckhove – also known as Wendy Van Wanten – with Laurent in 1996. Photonews via Getty Images Last year, Clément Vandenkerckhove appeared in a Belgian television documentary where he addressed his parentage and admitted to being Prince Laurent’s biological son. Laurent subsequently released an official statement confirming it, adding that he and his son had been having “open and honest conversations” in private in recent years to address his paternity.



In 2020, Princess Delphine, a Belgian artist, earned her title after a fierce seven-year legal battle against King Albert II of Belgium, who abdicated in 2013. The saga included a court-ordered DNA test under threat of a €5000 ($8000) daily fine. During the peak of her long-disputed paternity, the artist defiantly created art installations emblazoned with “Love Child” and “F--- You, I Exist”. Belgium’s Queen Mathilde with King Philippe in 2021. AP In 2018, the state reduced Prince Laurent’s annual allowance by 15 per cent (about €46,000) after he arrived at a Chinese embassy reception in full military uniform and tweeted a photo from the event without permission. That came after years of rogue diplomatic excursions, including an unauthorised 2011 visit to the Democratic Republic of Congo – a former Belgian colony – and a private sit-down in Libya with Muammar Gaddafi’s regime.



He also holds the unique distinction of being the first modern Belgian royal dragged into court as a witness in a fraud trial. Navy officers were accused of siphoning about €2 million in state funds, with more than €175,000 quietly funnelled into renovating Laurent’s Villa Clémentine and funding his animal welfare charity. Prince Laurent, left with his son, Clément. Instagram He claimed to have no idea where the funds came from, though he promised to reimburse the money. As he was never charged as a defendant, there was no formal acquittal. On Belgian National Day in 2019, the prince casually answered a phone call mid-national anthem while seated alongside other royals, drawing icy glares from his wife.



Related Article Royalty Daughter of Belgium's former king wins long battle to become princess He also once took the Belgian state to court demanding full social security benefits, medical reimbursements and sick pay on top of his annual royal endowment. He frequently complains about public life, once quipping to a group of schoolchildren that he could organise “the paratroopers to stage a coup at the palace”. World.title: This Sydney motorway was set to open in 2028. Now there’s no date
World.content:
The NSW roads minister has admitted there is no completion date for the $3 billion M6 motorway in Sydney’s south, despite earlier advice from the state’s transport agency that it would open to motorists by late 2028 as work was more than 90 per cent complete.

Jenny Aitchison told the NSW upper house’s budget estimates committee on Friday that there was no opening date for the four-kilometre underground motorway between Arncliffe and Kogarah, which has been stalled by years-long delays and a stand-off between the government and the contractors. The stalemate ended in June when contractors agreed to resume major work on the final section, more than two years after a 10-metre-wide sinkhole opened up.

Workers fill in a large sinkhole with cement in March 2024 to stabilise a two-storey building that had teetered on the edge. Rhett Wyman

“At this stage, we don’t [have a date]. We’ve agreed with the contractor that they’ll optimise the delivery as much as they can. They’re on-site, and we’re working with them to do that,” Aitchison said.

Transport for NSW’s previous target date for the M6’s completion was the end of 2028, which is three years later than a previously planned opening in late 2025. But following questions from the Herald, the agency confirmed on Friday that a completion date has not existed ever since work on the motorway recommenced in June.

World.title: Huge cocaine bust sparked by drugs floating in water
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Huge cocaine bust sparked by drugs floating in water Laine Clark August 21, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two men have been charged as part of an ongoing probe into Australia’s largest cocaine seizure. A firearm seized by police during a raid in Sydney. PR Handout/Supplied by the AFP Brisbane man Richard Huynh, 41, has been arrested after being accused of facilitating the shipment of almost three tonnes of cocaine from Queensland to NSW and Victoria through a transport business. A 23-year-old Sydney man has been also been accused of being part of a criminal syndicate after allegedly being found with a semi-automatic 9mm pistol and a loaded sawn-off shotgun along with ammunition and a silencer. He faces a string of firearms and drug charges as Operation Minjiang continues.



A total of 12 people now remain before Queensland and NSW courts in relation to the ongoing operation launched three months ago. It was triggered by the discovery of 40 kilograms of cocaine floating in the water, close to a burnt-out truck at Midge Point near Mackay on the central Queensland coast on May 30. Related Article Drugs Men charged, ‘mother vessel’ seized in multimillion-dollar drug-smuggling ring It led to Australian Federal Police uncovering a stash of 2.7 tonnes of cocaine under shipping containers in western Sydney on June 19. Officers discovered the drugs, with an estimated value of $816 million, buried under the false flooring.



It was the biggest Australian drug bust in nearly 20 years, and second only to the seizure of 4.5 tonnes of MDMA in Melbourne in 2007. Another of the seized firearms. AFP and Queensland Police officers executed a search warrant at a Kangaroo Point home, seizing $80,000 in cash and electronic devices. PR Handout/Supplied by the AFP Huynh was charged after a Kangaroo Point home was searched and $80,000 in cash and electronic devices was seized. Several electronic devices were also seized for digital forensic analysis, police said. Australian Federal Police allege other syndicate members moved 2.78 tonnes of cocaine from a suspected safehouse in Brisbane’s north to a Loganholme location in the city’s south.



Huynh is accused of facilitating the interstate shipment of the cocaine from Loganholme through the trucking logistics business before the drugs were moved to Sydney’s west. “The logistics business is not believed to have any involvement or knowledge of the offending,” Australian Federal Police said on Friday. A torched truck found at a north Queensland boat ramp near where 40 kilograms of cocaine was allegedly located in May. AFP Huynh was arrested at Brisbane airport on Thursday and charged with a number of offences. His matter appeared in Brisbane Magistrates Court on Friday.



He did not apply for bail and his matter was adjourned to September 18. The Sydney man was charged on Thursday after an Erskine Park, NSW residence was searched. Officers seized the guns, ammunition and silencer along with about 28g of cocaine and about $10,000 in cash in suspected proceeds of crime. He has been charged with a number of firearms and drug offences and appeared in Penrith Local Court on Thursday. AAP

World.title: Full cost of Kyle and Jackie O’s legal battle revealed
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Full cost of Kyle and Jackie O’s legal battle revealed Calum Jaspan Updated August 21, 2026 — 3:34pm ,first published 10:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kyle Sandilands and Jackie “O” Henderson’s months-long legal battle with their former employer ARN has cost the radio company more than $17 million so far as it battles rapidly declining revenue and profits. ARN Media revealed the figure – largely attributed to a $12 million settlement with Sandilands and bound to increase in October when it fights Henderson’s $82 million contract claim in the Federal Court – in its half-year results on Friday. The company posted a loss of $28.3 million for the half year and revenue that declined by 14 per cent to $128 million. Jackie “O” Henderson and Kyle Sandilands’ legal fights have dragged down ARN’s results. Chief executive Michael Stephenson said he wanted to see audiences and advertisers return to ARN’s KIIS radio station after a two-year boycott campaign from activists over Sandilands and a revolving door of fill-in hosts hindered ARN’s ability to bounce back. Well before Sandilands berated Henderson on air and reduced her to tears on February 20, ARN had a “long, long list of clients” that had specifically requested not to be advertised on KIIS Breakfast, Stephenson said.



“Because those clients didn’t advertise on KIIS breakfast, they often didn’t advertise with ARN at all,” Stephenson told this masthead after the earnings call. “Now, we have zero clients on any list, so that’s the first step. But of course, it does take some time to recover the lost ground.” The KIIS network has cycled through a number of interim hosts since Sandilands and Henderson’s departure. Permanent replacements will be announced imminently, Stephenson said, and new line-ups for both the Melbourne and Sydney breakfast shows will be revealed and on air before Christmas. Both he and chairman Hamish McLennan have been under pressure from shareholders, evidenced by the 90 per cent protest vote against the proposed remuneration package for executives in May. ARN will suspend dividends until its outstanding legal dispute with Henderson is resolved. Actions taken by ARN over the past 18 months have established a “stronger foundation for improved performance and long-term shareholder value”, McLennan said in a statement.



McLennan green-lit a 10-year, $200 million contract to keep The Kyle and Jackie O Show on KIIS FM in 2023 before Stephenson’s arrival. But the show blew up earlier this year following poor ratings in Melbourne, action from the media watchdog, the advertiser boycott and the deteriorating on-air relationship between Henderson and Sandilands. Since Stephenson joined the company last year, the former Nine Entertainment executive’s challenge has been to clean up the mess caused by the deal and arrest declining revenue. He could not be drawn to confirm any of the “stars” expected to host its breakfast shows, including speculation that Dr Chris Brown, known as the “Bondi Vet”, would replace Sandilands in Sydney. Stephenson said he was “not naive enough” to think ratings and advertisers would return overnight and said the opportunities in Sydney, where KIIS’ breakfast show had been the “absolute leader by a long way”, and Melbourne, where they were coming “dead pan last”, were very different. “I’m very confident that we will regain the [market] share that we’ve lost,” he said. “I don’t think [rival radio companies] Southern Cross and Nova really won much from us. I think we lost it.” The new show in Victoria will be “innovative and experimental” and “very Melbourne”, Stephenson said.



On the financials, Stephenson said ARN had made “strong progress” in stabilising its core business and strengthening its position, both by settling its matter with Sandilands and agreeing to sell its Hong Kong-based outdoor advertising business Cody. After the on-air feud in February, Henderson walked off the show and did not return. She informed ARN she could no longer work with her co-host and her contract was terminated. She is now suing the network, alleging it failed to protect her from Sandilands and improperly tore up her contract with $82 million left owing over several years. ARN also terminated Sandilands’ contract for allegedly bullying Henderson, which he denied. After settling the lawsuit, Sandilands told this masthead that ARN was a “house of cards”. Hundreds of staff have been made redundant and its share price has fallen about 44 per cent over the past 12 months to 26¢. “I don’t regret saying the comments to Jackie because it needed to be said,” Sandilands has said. “If it brought on an early exit from the show and the implosion of that show, then that’s unfortunate. But what are we supposed to do? Just pretend here for the rest of the nine years that everything’s fine?”

World.title: No review of BMD stadium contract after bikie link airing: Bleijie
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandBuilding Bad No review of BMD stadium contract after bikie link airing: Bleijie Matt Dennien August 21, 2026 — 4:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland’s deputy premier and infrastructure minister claims his government was not aware of alleged links between a major firm and a bikie standover on a taxpayer-funded construction site before it was handed lucrative Olympic stadium work. Speaking to media on Friday, Jarrod Bleijie played down evidence of the potentially illegal actions heard at the inquiry into the CFMEU and construction sector this week, while labelling them wrong, and said there would be no review of BMD’s contract for early works on the new Brisbane Stadium. He also brushed off comments from CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby, who called out the fact BMD had not removed the senior figures linked to the alleged incident and suspected cover-up, saying he would “not be lectured to by the CFMEU”. Jarrod Bleijie asked if “anyone [was] surprised that businesses were so desperate”, echoing comments from inquiry head Stuart Wood. Courtney Kruk The now $95-million, 28-month state-commissioned probe – following this masthead’s reporting on allegations of corruption and criminality in the nation’s construction sector – this week heard extensive circumstantial evidence of the matter.





He noted the contract was awarded by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Co-ordination Authority. On whether government would review the contract in light of this week’s evidence, Bleijie said it would not. Related Article Building Bad Inquiry and CFMEU bosses seek answers and action over alleged bikie plot “What we will assure you of is this: that the infrastructure and construction sites going forward under this government are going to be safe and productive,” he said. Asked on Friday if he agreed with Crosby that the alleged behaviour aired this week was “morally repugnant”, Bleijie said any suggestion the administration was the good guys was “absolutely laughable”. “I’m not going to be lectured to by the CFMEU,” he said, while noting he did not condone the actions. “But as the commissioner says, is anyone surprised that businesses were so desperate?



“I think what you’ll see is exposed is the desperation businesses went to combat that sort of behaviour from the CFMEU. It’s wrong. It will be exposed. It’ll be uncomfortable for a lot of people. “But the people more responsible for this [are] Steven Miles and Annastacia Palaszczuk, Cameron Dick and Shannon Fentiman.” BMD has tipped $8160 into LNP coffers since the election. Bleijie said questions about returning those donations were for his party, and suggested reporters ask Labor if it would return CFMEU donations.
