World.title: ASX Runners of the Week: Genesis, Triton, Pure One & DXN
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: Genesis, Triton, Pure One & DXN Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd August 21, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The gold bugs are definitely back and beaming this week. After months of being whacked by months of war-induced inflationary pressures leading to a resilient US dollar, the shiny yellow metal came roaring back to life as cracks began appearing in the American economy. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Genesis Resource. July’s non-farm payrolls (non-seasonal jobs) unexpectedly went backwards in reporting this week, shedding 23,000 jobs and reinforcing the view that the world’s largest economy may finally be cooling. Traders immediately began scaling back expectations of further rate hikes, while bond markets staged an unexpected rally after the US Treasury quietly doubled its planned buybacks of long-dated debt in an attempt to steady the bond market.



The Government printing more money to add to the already-groaning weight of more than US$40 trillion (A$61 trillion) in national debt is never a good sign of prosperity. The result was a familiar one. The US dollar softened to a runny egg and gold exploded higher, surging to more than six per cent to US$4550 (A$6910). Copper, meanwhile, refused to give an inch, holding firm near US$6.50 (A$9.95) per pound as the market struggles amid chronic supply shortages, remaining a powerful long-term red metal driver. Back home, Australia’s own inflation architects were quietly celebrating a milestone of their own. Federal debt has now blown through the trillion-dollar mark, leaving taxpayers with the privilege of funding record government spending while somehow managing higher taxes, higher electricity prices and a cost-of-living crisis that seemingly adds more brainwash initiatives by the second. An unexpected, good news story of the week came in the final reprieve for the ASX’s healthcare index, which was up a staggering 14 per cent in just one week. Former market darling and once Australia’s largest listed company, CSL, has had a ripping week after the healthcare giant spent the past year being treated like a biotech penny dreadful, shedding almost $90 billion in value from its highs. Investors finally decided enough was enough. The stock exploded nearly 18 per cent in a single session after management delivered better-than-expected FY26 numbers and forecasts for the year to come.



The resources sector also continued to remind everyone where Australia’s real economic engine sits BHP surged almost seven per cent as copper held its ground as the market’s metal of choice, while New Zealand’s biggest precious metals producer, OceanaGold, lobbed a hefty $776 million bid for Ausgold’s Katanning gold project in Western Australia. It seems OceanaGold, unable to expand its considerable resource base in NZ thanks to the government’s insistence on ignoring its own mineral wealth, has decided it’s time to expand into WA. The message is clear: quality ounces are making the big players move and they’re no longer waiting for developers to build the mines themselves. The Bulls N’ Bears Runners cavalcade this week perfectly mirrored the renewed gold sentiment, with the precious metal once again stamping its authority on the list. Pay-outs and payloads were the themes of the week for the minors, with a plucky gas explorer also making a late charge after plunging a well into one of Queensland’s most prolific gas basins. GENESIS RESOURCES LTD (ASX: GES) Up 500% (0.5c – 3c)



The Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is Genesis Resources, which took off in spectacular fashion this week after returning rock chip grades of up to 28.8 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from reconnaissance sampling at its Arltunga copper-gold project in the Northern Territory. Now, high-grade gold samples from surface are always going to get the market’s attention, but one struggles to recall too many occasions where a handful of rock chips have ignited a 500 per cent share price rally. Genesis rocketed to a high of 3c this week – its highest point in almost a decade. With gold back in favour and the company’s tightly held share register acting as an amplifier for every buy order, it was the perfect storm for this feisty junior to claim the top spot. The company collected 53 reconnaissance samples from previously undrilled areas across its exploration licence 100 kilometres northeast of Alice Springs, with standout results coming from the newly identified WP-10 prospect, where separate samples returned impressive assays of 11.25g/t and 10.47g/t gold. Along trend at Genesis’ Star Creek prospect, samples also delivered grades at an impressive 13.71g/t and 6.41g/t gold from around historical workings that include old trenches and a 10-metre-deep shaft, all crying out to be tested at depth. Even the company’s Jenkins Mine, which returned modest surface grades of up to 0.88g/t gold, comes with a tantalising backstory. Historical records from the Northern Territory Geological Survey suggest the mine once operated at an average head grade of a hefty 34.7g/t gold, which is yet to be tested by modern exploration.



With a clutch of high-grade targets now in hand, Genesis plans to drill-test WP-10, Star Creek, Chinaman’s Workings and Jenkins during the 2027 field season. The company also added a tasty kicker, collecting 10 rock-chip samples from previously untested areas on its Alice Springs tenement before unseasonal rain brought the field program to an early end. One of those samples returned 1.2 per cent copper roughly 300 metres northeast of the nearest drill hole at the Diana 2 prospect, with follow-up fieldwork now planned. Gold and copper remain two of the hottest commodities in town, and Genesis appears to have a solid footing in both. The market has already cast its vote on the surface results. Now comes the real test – whether those flashy grades can survive the journey from a rock on the surface to a drill core at depth. TRITON MINERALS LTD (ASX: TON) Up 100% (0.25c – 0.5c) Stealing second place this week is Triton Minerals, whose shares doubled after the company finally drew a line under a long-running dispute and secured a pathway to complete the sale of a 70 per cent stake in its Mozambique graphite assets.



A new deed of settlement has now resolved the legal proceedings that stemmed from its partner, NQM Gold 2 Pty Ltd, missing staged payments under the original agreement, which was worth about $17 million. Under the latest deal, the transaction will complete on August 21, with Triton set to receive the remaining $5.5 million held in trust. NQM will take ownership of 70 per cent of the assets, while Triton will retain a substantial 30 per cent stake in the joint venture. Accordingly, court proceedings will now be discontinued. The market’s excitement is understandable given the sheer scale of the graphite assets involved. Triton’s flagship Ancuabe project hosts a JORC mineral resource of 46 million tonnes grading 6.6 per cent total graphitic carbon for 3.04 million tonnes of contained graphite. A definitive feasibility study has already outlined a production profile of 60,000 tonnes of graphite concentrate per year over a mine life stretching almost three decades, involving a valuable mix of large and jumbo graphite flakes. The bigger prize, however, may well be the Cobra Plains deposit.Hosting a massive inferred resource of 103 million tonnes grading 5.2 per cent total graphitic carbon for a staggering 5.7 million tonnes of contained graphite, the asset also benefits from sitting within a 25-year mining concession. Combined, the Mozambique assets contain almost 9 million tonnes of graphite resources, making them among the biggest undeveloped graphite inventories on the ASX. With environmental approvals, mining concessions and development studies already in place, the market appears to be betting that this settlement finally clears the path for the projects to move from courtroom battles to mine development.



With legal clarification, a booming graphite market and $5.5 million in cash on its way, Triton’s story looks like it can finally get back on track. A Silver City rig drilling Pure One’s Venus-2H well in the prolific Surat Basin, in Queensland. PURE ONE CORP LTD (ASX: P1E) Up 91% (3.3c – 6.3c) We love a late runner at Bulls N’ Bears, and junior energy hopeful Pure One Corp has made a late dash for the final podium spot on Friday.



The company announced strong gas shows at its Venus-2H horizontal appraisal well in Queensland’s Surat Basin, with total gas readings hitting up to 25.4 per cent as drilling continues towards its intersection with the Venus-1 wellbore. Project Venus is a first-rate asset because it sits in the heart of Queensland’s premier Walloon Fairway, the most proven and productive coal-seam gas province in the state. This area has already seen more than 10,000 wells drilled and supplies the bulk of the gas that feeds the LNG export facilities at Gladstone. The permit is surrounded by major operators such as Origin, Apollo, Arrow, QGC and Santos, meaning the geology is well understood, the infrastructure is dense and commercial pathways are already established. The current Venus-2 well is an appraisal, commercial-style horizontal well designed to prove gas deliverability. It has been drilled vertically to about 420m, before turning horizontal for approximately 1km. It will then intersect the existing Venus-1 well for dewatering, followed by flow testing. Every previous well on the block has already produced gas to surface, giving management high confidence. The implications for Pure One are compelling. The junior explorer retains a controlling 69.4 per cent stake in Eastern Gas Corporation, the listed vehicle that now holds and funds the project. A successful commercial flow test would therefore deliver a material uplift in value directly to Pure One’s balance sheet and share price, without the company having to fund the full development itself. New domestic and exportable gas supply is definitely back from the doldrums in Australia and proving a commercial resource in this location could rapidly re-rate Pure One.



The discovery could transform from a pure junior explorer into a company with a de-risked, infrastructure-adjacent gas asset - a powerful catalyst sitting comfortably alongside its additional technology, which is focused on an EV-vehicle launch planned for next month. The company recently rebranded from Pure Hydrogen to Pure One to reflect its expansion into battery-electric and multi-technology clean mobility solutions. The focus is on capital-light, partner-manufactured vehicles using proven components, targeting commercial and government fleets where battery-swap technology is especially attractive. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… DXN Limited. DXN LIMITED (ASX: DXN) Up 35% (21.5c – 29c)



Rounding out our runners list is Bulls N’ Bears regular DXN Limited. While its 35 per cent gain for the week was modest compared to the others, the broader story for this data centre specialist is astounding. The company announced that it had been awarded a contract by Australia Pacific Airports, the operator of Melbourne Airport. Under the agreement, DXN will design, manufacture, deliver, install and commission a prefabricated Edge Data Centre facility, with the contract valued at approximately $4.1 million. This comes on the heels of an $8.8 million deal inked recently with a US Neo-Cloud operator, which could be worth up to US$200 million (A$280M) in future orders. DXN’s point of difference in the data-centre world lies in its speed-to-deployment, modular scalability and direct liquid cooling expertise. Subject to successful delivery, the Melbourne Airport operator has indicated its intent to progress to a substantially larger campus program, representing a potential revenue opportunity for DXN well in excess of US$200 million for the existing site in the next one to two years. Airports operate a dense mix of latency-sensitive, safety-critical systems that increasingly require compute and network capacity to be physically located near the operations they serve, rather than being housed in a distant central facility. The award builds on DXN’s track record of delivering prefabricated critical infrastructure for government, telecommunications and blue-chip enterprise customers across the Asia Pacific. With its share price now up nearly 1300 per cent since its lows in May, DXN is once again raising its hand to be in contention for Runners of the Year 2026 glory when it is all said and done. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Fourth Sydney Airport safety incident under investigation in as many weeks
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Fourth Sydney Airport safety incident under investigation in as many weeks Chris Zappone Updated August 21, 2026 — 3:45pm ,first published 11:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Investigators are examining how two Qantas flights at Sydney Airport were given clearance to take the same route on a taxiway on Tuesday. The incident is the fourth in the past four weeks at the airport, where shortages of air traffic controllers in its tower are being blamed for frequent delays. A Qantas 737 at Sydney Airport in a file photo. Wolter Peeters The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said a Qantas 737 arriving from the Gold Coast was heading west on the ground and had clearance to turn right. At the same time, a Qantas Airbus A321 preparing to depart for Melbourne also had clearance to turn, which would have put it in the other plane’s path.



“As the Airbus approached ... the crew observed the Boeing approaching from the left and stopped the aircraft,” the bureau said. Related Article Aviation Sydney Airport has had three close calls in as many weeks. The first big problem is clear Scrutiny over the operations of air traffic controllers has increased in the past month, following a series of incidents primarily at Sydney Airport. The safety bureau is also investigating a runway incursion and a rejected take-off of Virgin Australia flight VA555 from Sydney to Perth and Qantas flight QF728 from Sydney to Ayers Rock Airport on August 9. On the same day, a Jetstar A320 almost collided with a Qatar Airways Boeing 777. That incident was initially described as a near collision, although the bureau later called it a “proximity event”.



On the latest investigation, on August 18, the bureau said: “The evidence collection phase of the investigation will involve interviewing involved air traffic controllers and flight crew, retrieving and reviewing available recorded data, and the collection of other relevant information.” The bureau said in a statement it would look at the instructions given to flight crews and whether there were common factors with the spate of other incidents at Sydney Airport. There was no immediate risk of collision, it said, as the Qantas A321 aircraft was braking normally before coming to a stop. The bureau classified the event as a safety “incident” rather than a “serious incident”. It will conduct an investigation “to understand the potential conflicting instructions to the flight crews and whether there are any contributing factors common across the other Sydney Airport incidents currently under investigation”. A Qantas spokesperson said: “Our aircraft was cleared to proceed following instructions from air traffic control and we will support the ATSB in the investigation.”



Airservices Australia, the government-owned body in charge of air traffic control, said it reported the August 18 incident to the bureau as “involving a potential traffic conflict between two Qantas aircraft taxiing on the ground using the taxiway system”. The smooth operation of Sydney Airport’s tower has been the source of concern from the airline industry, which has complained about regular delays at the major airport. iStock Airservices described the report as part of its safety management system process. ”As with all reported occurrences, we will provide the bureau with all relevant information and act on any findings arising from its investigation,” an Airservices spokesperson said. “The recent ground traffic incidents currently under investigation by the bureau involve a range of circumstances, and each incident is being investigated on its individual facts.



Related Article Editorial

Airports We’re used to airport queues and delays, but safety is not negotiable The Herald's View Editorial “Airservices will continue to review operational events and take any action required to maintain safe operations.” The smooth operation of Sydney Airport’s tower has been the source of concern from the airline industry, which has complained about regular delays at the major airport. Some air traffic controllers have expressed concern over increased workload related to the opening of Western Sydney International. On July 27, a QantasLink flight and a Qantas flight were involved in a near miss on the tarmac in Sydney.



The incidents have raised concern about the staffing at Sydney’s air traffic control tower, which is under increasing pressure. Airservices said that in 12 months to July 2025, the bureau had received more than 14,600 aviation notifications from across the industry. Airservices submits multiple reports to the ATSB daily “as part of regular operational procedure”. University of Sydney professor Rico Merkert said for many instances involving towing vehicles or activity on the taxiway, the impact of an incident potentially “wouldn’t be that large”. “But having said that, recently there have been at least a couple, where the impact would be actually quite significant.” Deploying more sensors helped decision-makers focus on keeping planes safe, Merkert said. “The closer you get to the gate, the more you can automate the decision-making.



“I think the lot can be done there to improve the current processes and make it easier for the decision maker.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: This footy president wants to stamp out inequality and misogyny in sport. She’s running for parliament
World.content:
Exclusive SportVictorian election This footy president wants to stamp out inequality and misogyny in sport. She’s running for parliament Hannah Kennelly August 21, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Natalie Korinfsky stood “up to the blokes” at her football club. Now the president of the Wedge-Tailed Eagles – formerly known as the Kyneton Women’s Football Club – is running for Victorian parliament at a time when poor behaviour in sport is in the national spotlight. The Animal Justice Party has announced Natalie Korinfsky as its candidate for the seat of Macedon in the state election. Joe Armao Korinfsky led a high-profile battle for the Kyneton women’s right to play after they defected from their previous club following claims over inequitable treatment and disrespectful conditions. She has announced her candidacy in the upcoming state election for the Animal Justice Party in the seat of Macedon, which is held for Labor by retiring health minister Mary-Anne Thomas.





Purcell, who has been a prominent voice on women’s rights and against sexism herself, said Korinfsky’s decision to stand for parliament could not be more important. “For Natalie and her team of incredible women to not only stand up to the blokes at their club - but also the boys club that is the AFL - is nothing short of inspiring,” she said. “These are exactly the type of people that we need to see elected to our halls of power. “That is why Natalie running for parliament matters. We need people with lived experience of these environments at the table when laws are made to ensure that women’s safety isn’t just a buzz word. “Women shouldn’t have to fight this hard just to be heard. But when they do, we need to make sure they are given a seat at the table.”



Korinfsky told this masthead she would draw on her experiences in combatting discrimination in grassroots sports, focusing on standing up for those whose voices are often overlooked. Like many others, she added, she felt disheartened by the major parties for the upcoming election in November and wanted to bring more compassion to politics. Kyneton Women’s football team, now known as the Wedge-Tailed Eagles. Joe Armao “It’s probably something I never imagined doing,” she said. “With the state of politics, I think sometimes you just have to do things that are a little bit scary to try and enact some change.” Korinfsky is a social worker with experience in youth mental health and disability support, and has recently worked for Omnia Community Health, running programs to keep young people in education. She also wants to improve the state of community sporting facilities in Macedon.



She will be running against Labor candidate Annette Death and former Macedon Ranges mayor Kate Kendall, who will represent the Liberals. While she did not comment specifically on the Swans, Korinfsky said it was important to see strong leadership from the AFL and other sports, to encourage systematic change. “We’re not seeing our big sporting organisations and our government really come down on gender-based violence and sexism, misogyny,” she said. “Then how do we expect our sporting clubs on the ground to really know what to do?” MP Georgie Purcell (left) and Natalie Korinfsk



Purcell said if re-elected to parliament, the Animal Justice Party wanted to establish a state parliamentary inquiry into equity and inclusion in sport, and hear from communities about their experiences in sport, “whether that be sexism, homophobia, transphobia or racism”. Purcell was a vocal supporter of the Wedge-Tailed Eagles during their search for a league to play in, after the breakaway team’s application to the Central Victorian league was initially blocked by their former league, Riddell. In February, this masthead revealed that the vice-president of the Riddell District Football Netball League, Andrew Power, had resigned following a series of questions from The Age to the league about vulgar comments Power had left on the women’s team’s Instagram page. Shortly after, the AFL announced Kyneton Women’s Football Club could play in the Central Victorian Football League this season after 12 months in limbo under their new name, the Wedge-Tailed Eagles. When Purcell extended her support, she said she heard from many women from other sporting clubs in similar predicaments.



“Obviously, the Wedgies really set a standard and were incredibly brave and put their faces to it. But the reality is, so many people are afraid to even speak out, and we need to provide that forum for people to do so safely and perhaps confidentially to address this really serious and systemic problem,” she said. World.title: This 26-year-old former car salesman just quietly became a European prince
World.content:
WorldEuropeBelgium This 26-year-old former car salesman just quietly became a European prince Lilia Sebouai August 21, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man has become a prince at the age of 26 after the brother of the king of Belgium finally recognised him as his own. Prince Laurent is the brother of King Philippe and has long been labelled the “cursed prince” of the Saxe-Coburg house. Clément Vandenkerckhove in Jaunuary. Alamy Stock Photo He has registered his paternity of Clément Vandenkerckhove with the civil registry. Vandenkerckhove was born to Iris Vandenkerckhove – better known as singer, actress and socialite Wendy Van Wanten – before Prince Laurent’s 2003 marriage to Princess Claire, with whom he shares three children.



While civil recognition makes the former car salesman a prince and gives him equal inheritance rights to Prince Laurent’s private estate alongside his half-siblings, the royal perks stop there. Owing to Belgium’s 2013 royal endowment reforms, public funding is strictly limited to the reigning monarch and the direct heir. He will not be given a state stipend or official duties, and has zero rights to the throne. Belgium’s Princess Claire and Prince Laurent during National Day celebrations in July. Getty Images Laurent met Iris Vandenkerckhove at a Paris fashion show in the mid-90s and began a high-profile relationship. When their son was born in August 2000, the Belgian press immediately speculated about his paternity.



The name Clément was widely read as a direct nod to Villa Clémentine, Prince Laurent’s official residence in Tervuren, a Flemish town just outside Brussels. Iris Vandenkerckhove also repeatedly hinted at hidden lovers in several of her pop ballads. Iris Vandenkerckhove – also known as Wendy Van Wanten – with Laurent in 1996. Photonews via Getty Images Last year, Clément Vandenkerckhove appeared in a Belgian television documentary where he addressed his parentage and admitted to being Prince Laurent’s biological son. Laurent subsequently released an official statement confirming it, adding that he and his son had been having “open and honest conversations” in private in recent years to address his paternity.



In 2020, Princess Delphine, a Belgian artist, earned her title after a fierce seven-year legal battle against King Albert II of Belgium, who abdicated in 2013. The saga included a court-ordered DNA test under threat of a €5000 ($8000) daily fine. During the peak of her long-disputed paternity, the artist defiantly created art installations emblazoned with “Love Child” and “F--- You, I Exist”. Belgium’s Queen Mathilde with King Philippe in 2021. AP In 2018, the state reduced Prince Laurent’s annual allowance by 15 per cent (about €46,000) after he arrived at a Chinese embassy reception in full military uniform and tweeted a photo from the event without permission. That came after years of rogue diplomatic excursions, including an unauthorised 2011 visit to the Democratic Republic of Congo – a former Belgian colony – and a private sit-down in Libya with Muammar Gaddafi’s regime.



He also holds the unique distinction of being the first modern Belgian royal dragged into court as a witness in a fraud trial. Navy officers were accused of siphoning about €2 million in state funds, with more than €175,000 quietly funnelled into renovating Laurent’s Villa Clémentine and funding his animal welfare charity. Prince Laurent, left with his son, Clément. Instagram He claimed to have no idea where the funds came from, though he promised to reimburse the money. As he was never charged as a defendant, there was no formal acquittal. On Belgian National Day in 2019, the prince casually answered a phone call mid-national anthem while seated alongside other royals, drawing icy glares from his wife.



Related Article Royalty Daughter of Belgium's former king wins long battle to become princess He also once took the Belgian state to court demanding full social security benefits, medical reimbursements and sick pay on top of his annual royal endowment. He frequently complains about public life, once quipping to a group of schoolchildren that he could organise “the paratroopers to stage a coup at the palace”. World.title: This Sydney motorway was set to open in 2028. Now there’s no date
World.content:
The NSW roads minister has admitted there is no completion date for the $3 billion M6 motorway in Sydney’s south, despite earlier advice from the state’s transport agency that it would open to motorists by late 2028 as work was more than 90 per cent complete.

Jenny Aitchison told the NSW upper house’s budget estimates committee on Friday that there was no opening date for the four-kilometre underground motorway between Arncliffe and Kogarah, which has been stalled by years-long delays and a stand-off between the government and the contractors. The stalemate ended in June when contractors agreed to resume major work on the final section, more than two years after a 10-metre-wide sinkhole opened up.

Workers fill in a large sinkhole with cement in March 2024 to stabilise a two-storey building that had teetered on the edge. Rhett Wyman

“At this stage, we don’t [have a date]. We’ve agreed with the contractor that they’ll optimise the delivery as much as they can. They’re on-site, and we’re working with them to do that,” Aitchison said.

Transport for NSW’s previous target date for the M6’s completion was the end of 2028, which is three years later than a previously planned opening in late 2025. But following questions from the Herald, the agency confirmed on Friday that a completion date has not existed ever since work on the motorway recommenced in June.

World.title: Huge cocaine bust sparked by drugs floating in water
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Huge cocaine bust sparked by drugs floating in water Laine Clark August 21, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two men have been charged as part of an ongoing probe into Australia’s largest cocaine seizure. A firearm seized by police during a raid in Sydney. PR Handout/Supplied by the AFP Brisbane man Richard Huynh, 41, has been arrested after being accused of facilitating the shipment of almost three tonnes of cocaine from Queensland to NSW and Victoria through a transport business. A 23-year-old Sydney man has been also been accused of being part of a criminal syndicate after allegedly being found with a semi-automatic 9mm pistol and a loaded sawn-off shotgun along with ammunition and a silencer. He faces a string of firearms and drug charges as Operation Minjiang continues.



A total of 12 people now remain before Queensland and NSW courts in relation to the ongoing operation launched three months ago. It was triggered by the discovery of 40 kilograms of cocaine floating in the water, close to a burnt-out truck at Midge Point near Mackay on the central Queensland coast on May 30. Related Article Drugs Men charged, ‘mother vessel’ seized in multimillion-dollar drug-smuggling ring It led to Australian Federal Police uncovering a stash of 2.7 tonnes of cocaine under shipping containers in western Sydney on June 19. Officers discovered the drugs, with an estimated value of $816 million, buried under the false flooring.



It was the biggest Australian drug bust in nearly 20 years, and second only to the seizure of 4.5 tonnes of MDMA in Melbourne in 2007. Another of the seized firearms. AFP and Queensland Police officers executed a search warrant at a Kangaroo Point home, seizing $80,000 in cash and electronic devices. PR Handout/Supplied by the AFP Huynh was charged after a Kangaroo Point home was searched and $80,000 in cash and electronic devices was seized. Several electronic devices were also seized for digital forensic analysis, police said. Australian Federal Police allege other syndicate members moved 2.78 tonnes of cocaine from a suspected safehouse in Brisbane’s north to a Loganholme location in the city’s south.



Huynh is accused of facilitating the interstate shipment of the cocaine from Loganholme through the trucking logistics business before the drugs were moved to Sydney’s west. “The logistics business is not believed to have any involvement or knowledge of the offending,” Australian Federal Police said on Friday. A torched truck found at a north Queensland boat ramp near where 40 kilograms of cocaine was allegedly located in May. AFP Huynh was arrested at Brisbane airport on Thursday and charged with a number of offences. His matter appeared in Brisbane Magistrates Court on Friday.



He did not apply for bail and his matter was adjourned to September 18. The Sydney man was charged on Thursday after an Erskine Park, NSW residence was searched. Officers seized the guns, ammunition and silencer along with about 28g of cocaine and about $10,000 in cash in suspected proceeds of crime. He has been charged with a number of firearms and drug offences and appeared in Penrith Local Court on Thursday. AAP

World.title: Full cost of Kyle and Jackie O’s legal battle revealed
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Full cost of Kyle and Jackie O’s legal battle revealed Calum Jaspan Updated August 21, 2026 — 3:34pm ,first published 10:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kyle Sandilands and Jackie “O” Henderson’s months-long legal battle with their former employer ARN has cost the radio company more than $17 million so far as it battles rapidly declining revenue and profits. ARN Media revealed the figure – largely attributed to a $12 million settlement with Sandilands and bound to increase in October when it fights Henderson’s $82 million contract claim in the Federal Court – in its half-year results on Friday. The company posted a loss of $28.3 million for the half year and revenue that declined by 14 per cent to $128 million. Jackie “O” Henderson and Kyle Sandilands’ legal fights have dragged down ARN’s results. Chief executive Michael Stephenson said he wanted to see audiences and advertisers return to ARN’s KIIS radio station after a two-year boycott campaign from activists over Sandilands and a revolving door of fill-in hosts hindered ARN’s ability to bounce back. Well before Sandilands berated Henderson on air and reduced her to tears on February 20, ARN had a “long, long list of clients” that had specifically requested not to be advertised on KIIS Breakfast, Stephenson said.



“Because those clients didn’t advertise on KIIS breakfast, they often didn’t advertise with ARN at all,” Stephenson told this masthead after the earnings call. “Now, we have zero clients on any list, so that’s the first step. But of course, it does take some time to recover the lost ground.” The KIIS network has cycled through a number of interim hosts since Sandilands and Henderson’s departure. Permanent replacements will be announced imminently, Stephenson said, and new line-ups for both the Melbourne and Sydney breakfast shows will be revealed and on air before Christmas. Both he and chairman Hamish McLennan have been under pressure from shareholders, evidenced by the 90 per cent protest vote against the proposed remuneration package for executives in May. ARN will suspend dividends until its outstanding legal dispute with Henderson is resolved. Actions taken by ARN over the past 18 months have established a “stronger foundation for improved performance and long-term shareholder value”, McLennan said in a statement.



McLennan green-lit a 10-year, $200 million contract to keep The Kyle and Jackie O Show on KIIS FM in 2023 before Stephenson’s arrival. But the show blew up earlier this year following poor ratings in Melbourne, action from the media watchdog, the advertiser boycott and the deteriorating on-air relationship between Henderson and Sandilands. Since Stephenson joined the company last year, the former Nine Entertainment executive’s challenge has been to clean up the mess caused by the deal and arrest declining revenue. He could not be drawn to confirm any of the “stars” expected to host its breakfast shows, including speculation that Dr Chris Brown, known as the “Bondi Vet”, would replace Sandilands in Sydney. Stephenson said he was “not naive enough” to think ratings and advertisers would return overnight and said the opportunities in Sydney, where KIIS’ breakfast show had been the “absolute leader by a long way”, and Melbourne, where they were coming “dead pan last”, were very different. “I’m very confident that we will regain the [market] share that we’ve lost,” he said. “I don’t think [rival radio companies] Southern Cross and Nova really won much from us. I think we lost it.” The new show in Victoria will be “innovative and experimental” and “very Melbourne”, Stephenson said.



On the financials, Stephenson said ARN had made “strong progress” in stabilising its core business and strengthening its position, both by settling its matter with Sandilands and agreeing to sell its Hong Kong-based outdoor advertising business Cody. After the on-air feud in February, Henderson walked off the show and did not return. She informed ARN she could no longer work with her co-host and her contract was terminated. She is now suing the network, alleging it failed to protect her from Sandilands and improperly tore up her contract with $82 million left owing over several years. ARN also terminated Sandilands’ contract for allegedly bullying Henderson, which he denied. After settling the lawsuit, Sandilands told this masthead that ARN was a “house of cards”. Hundreds of staff have been made redundant and its share price has fallen about 44 per cent over the past 12 months to 26¢. “I don’t regret saying the comments to Jackie because it needed to be said,” Sandilands has said. “If it brought on an early exit from the show and the implosion of that show, then that’s unfortunate. But what are we supposed to do? Just pretend here for the rest of the nine years that everything’s fine?”

World.title: IRD still talking to charities about cap on donation tax credits: Luxon
World.content:
The Prime Minister says the Inland Revenue Department will continue to engage with the charitable sector on a policy to cap donation tax credits, after one of his MPs criticised the policy.

On Thursday, Maungakiekie MP Greg Fleming told a charity event that the government's plan to cap the donation tax credit had "zero" logic, and that work was under way to fix it.

Revenue Minister Simon Watts said that was not the case, and Fleming has admitted he misspoke.

"The minister is aware of concerns from some charities and philanthropists about the effect this change could have on charitable giving, and I understand IRD are continuing to engage with the sector on this," Fleming told RNZ.

On Friday, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he was aware there were concerns from the charitable sector.

"There's no change from a government point of view, but IRD are continuing to engage with the sector. I know there are some concerns from the charitable sector; that's why IRD will continue to engage with them."

Donors can claim a third of their charitable donations as a tax credit, but from April they will be unable to claim a credit once they give more than $100,000.

The charities sector has expressed concern that the cap may make would-be donors consider dialling back their donations at a time the sector was already struggling.

Inland Revenue has been concerned the tax credit could be misused for tax planning purposes, when a donor makes a gift to a charity they control themselves.

World.title: Lawyer convicted of assault on his 12-year-old son which left him hospitalised
World.content:
A lawyer has been convicted and granted name suppression following a serious assault on his son that required him being hospitalised.

The lawyer, aged in his 50s, appeared in the Timaru District Court on Friday before Judge Campbell Savage where he was sentenced to supervision after pleading guilty to a charge of assault on a child.

The judge said the case, which began in 2022, had moved at "glacial pace".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Court documents obtained by RNZ detail the offending which occurred in April 2022.

The summary of facts said the lawyer and his son were boxing on a concrete area at the rear of their address.

The lawyer was a "fully grown man and the victim is a small built, 38kg 12-year-old child," the summary said.

Both were wearing boxing gloves.

The lawyer struck the victim's head causing him to bleed.

"The victim said 'please stop. I am serious'.

"The defendant then struck the victim in the face followed by the stomach. This caused the victim to cry. He went to the ground.

"The defendant continued to punch the victim on the ground. Eventually the victim said he could not breath and the defendant stopped. The victim then jumped the fence to get away."

The victim was taken to hospital and was initially diagnosed with a suspected fractured cheekbone and perforated liver, however after scans this was not the case.

He sustained extensive bruising to his head and ears and a cut above his eye.

He was admitted to hospital for three nights to allow observation and investigation of his possible injuries.

The lawyer declined to comment to police.

At sentencing the man's lawyer, Michael Sandom told the court the lawyer appeared before the court as a defendant and as a practicing lawyer.

The lawyer was convicted at Timaru District Court. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Sandom said he was appearing among many of his colleagues and peers, which brought a level of "embarrassment and shame".

"[He] is not a perfect person, but none of us are.

"He knows the mistake that he made, he is remorseful for what occurred and in my submission shame for what occurred is an important theme for this sentencing."

Sandom said the offending would stay with the lawyer "for the rest of his life".

The offending was "distressing and repugnant" to the lawyer.

"He's ashamed for what occurred. He can barely face it, can barely talk about it, can barely engage with it at all."

Sandom said the lawyer was a "kind and generous person" as well as an "advocate" in the criminal jurisdiction.

He accepted it was "serious" offending.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae said the Crown opposed the lawyer's application for a discharge without conviction and said his affidavit for name suppression did not meet the threshold.

Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. (File photo) Stuff / Pool / Alden Williams

Judge Savage said the matter had passed through the court system "at glacial pace", with the first hearing in April 2022.

The lawyer pleaded guilty during a trial after the victim had given evidence. Judge Savage said the lawyer's claim he did not see his son's statement until trial was "implausible".

"One's led to the inescapable conclusion that you've done just about everything in your powers to frustrate the process, including avoiding the service of summons. It seems that you've used your knowledge of the system to duck and dive attempts to get it set down, and then you've counterpunched with a flurry of meritless pre-trial applications."

Judge Savage said it was "charitable" to say the lawyer's guilty plea came at the 11th hour.

"It came as the clock was striking 12."

He said he had no doubt the lawyer loved his son "with all your heart".

In terms of aggravating factors, the judge pointed to the victim's age and the breach of trust.

Judge Savage declined to discharge the lawyer without a conviction, but did grant final name suppression.

He said he did not see the lawyer as a risk of re-offending.

The lawyer has been practicing for more than a decade. The New Zealand Law Society register does not say whether he holds a practicing certificate.

RNZ asked the New Zealand Law Society how the lawyer was able to continue practicing while the matter was before the court.

A spokesperson said the Law Society took any concerns regarding criminal offending by lawyers "seriously".

"Personal conduct by a lawyer may be considered under the complaints and disciplinary framework in the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 (the Act) in certain circumstances.

"However, a lawyer who holds a current practising certificate and admits to, or is found guilty of, criminal offending is not automatically suspended from practice."

The spokesperson said concerns or complaints must first be considered by independent Standards Committees who may refer matters to the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal, if the conduct was "sufficiently serious".

"In addition, section 40 of the Act provides that a lawyer who has applied to renew their practising certificate may continue to practise while the application is being considered. This may include cases where proceedings are ongoing."

Asked if a lawyer could be suspended pending a complaint, the spokesperson said only the tribunal could make an order that a lawyer be suspended from practice, including for an interim period while any disciplinary process is underway, or strike a lawyer off the roll of barristers and solicitors following referral from a Standards Committee.

The Disciplinary Tribunal is administered by the Ministry of Justice.

Asked why the register did not have the expiry date for the lawyer's practising certificate, the spokesperson said the Society was unable to comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.

"Speaking generally, practising certificates have an expiry date of 30 June each year."

Ministry of Justice acting group manager of National Service Delivery Louisa Carroll said the Ministry could not comment on the circumstances of any individual lawyer or active court proceedings.

Asked about the lawyer receiving legal aid clients, Carroll said legal aid providers must meet and maintain approval requirements and comply with the Legal Services Act, their legal aid provider contract, and professional obligations.

"Legal aid providers are also required to notify the Ministry within five working days if they are charged with, or convicted of, an offence punishable by imprisonment."

"Where the Ministry becomes aware of concerns about a provider, it may consider those concerns through its complaints, audit, quality assurance and provider approval processes."

Carroll said depending on the circumstances, the Ministry may take a range of actions, including imposing restrictions on a provider, modifying or cancelling their approval to undertake legal aid work, or referring matters to the New Zealand Law Society.

"Approved providers remain eligible to receive legal aid assignments unless their approval is changed, restricted, suspended, or cancelled.

World.title: Third case of H5 bird flu found in Wellington region
World.content:
A third case of H5 bird flu has been detected in a northern giant petrel, in the Wairarapa.

Ministry for Primary Industries says it was found dead on a remote Cape Palliser beach.

It follows cases found in a kāhu, or swamp harrier, and a brown skua.

It was found by a Department of Conservation (DOC) ranger, who notified the MPI hotline.

Samples received by the MPI Animal Health Laboratory on 14 August were tested and initially found low levels of influenza virus in the bird. It took several rounds of testing to confirm bird flu.

MPI chief veterinary officer Mary van Andel says this hasn't come as a surprise as ocean-going birds can arrive on New Zealand coastlines.

Van Andel says the risk to human health remains low and there were no other signs of issues at the beach.

World.title: Police close Papatoetoe election fraud investigation due to insufficient evidence
World.content:
A 10-month police investigation into allegations of electoral fraud linked to the 2025 Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board election has been closed due to insufficient evidence.

The investigation began after complaints were made following the election, in which all four seats in the Papatoetoe subdivision were won by newcomers from the Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team.

"A thorough review was carried out into the complaints we received," said Detective Inspector Shaun Vickers, Counties Manukau CIB.

"Ultimately there was insufficient evidence to proceed further, when taking the Solicitor General's Prosecution Guidelines into account. All files have now been closed."

A spokesperson from the Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team welcomed the news.

"For our team, this brings an important chapter to a close," the spokesperson said.

"We believed throughout this process that justice and truth should be allowed to take their course," the spokesperson said.

"Sometimes that process takes longer than we would like, but our confidence in New Zealand's institutions has remained."

Police confirmed in October they were making enquiries into complaints of electoral fraud relating to the South Auckland local body election.

In November, a former Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board member filed a petition seeking a judicial inquiry into the election.

Labour candidate Lehopoaome Vi Hausia's petition raised concerns about turnout anomalies, the handling of ballot papers and the integrity of postal voting.

In December, Judge Richard McIlraith ruled that irregularities had materially affected the result and declared the election of the local board members for the Papatoetoe subdivision void.

A separate legal challenge followed in February, when four winning candidates from the voided election sought a judicial review in the High Court.

Following a hearing on 17 February, the High Court upheld the District Court's decision to void the result.

Justice Anderson also addressed social media comments suggesting the District Court's ruling demonstrated "immigrant corruption" and that the "Indian candidates masterminded fraudulent votes".

"This is a misleading and improper report of the decision," Justice Anderson said.

"Mr Hausia does not allege - nor did the [District Court] judge find - that [the Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team] had any involvement in the misuse of voting papers identified in the decision."

A new election was held in April.

Vi Hausia secured top spot in the new election, with three members of the Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team also claiming seats.

Vi Hausia received 2788 votes, followed by Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team candidate Jeet Singh on 2484.

Fellow Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team candidate Sandeep Saini received 2479 votes, while Kushma Nair won the fourth and final seat with 2383 votes.

World.title: Air New Zealand forced to BYO fuel due to contaminated batch in Fiji
World.content:
Air New Zealand is among several airlines carrying extra fuel and cancelling services as a response to fuel contamination in Fiji.

A spokesperson for the airline told RNZ that over the past two days measures had been taken to manage fuel restrictions in Fiji.

This included "tankering fuel, cancelling one service, and upgauging two services to our Widebody aircraft".

The spokesperson said affected passengers had been moved to other services departing the same day.

The airline would continue to minimise disruptions, they said.

The ABC reported both Qantas and Virgin Airlines were also forced to bring in excess fuel to make the return journey to Australia.

Virgin Australia on Thursday cancelled two services on its Fiji route, according to the ABC.

The airline confirmed planes were being forced to stop halfway at airports in New Caledonia and Vanuatu to make the journey back to Australia and Fiji.

Sources had told the ABC the contamination related to an excessive electrical charge in a batch of fuel stored at the airport.

The source indicated it could be resolved soon or escalate into a more significant issue.

The ABC also reported pilots had been told the problem may continue until the end of the month.

Fiji Airports did not confirm to the ABC the cause of the contamination issue.

A spokesperson said they were making "operational adjustments" and the airport was "closely monitoring the current aviation fuel situation".

"Nadi International Airport remains open and operational, with established safety and operational protocols being maintained," it told the ABC.

World.title: 'Doesn't bring Blake back' - inquest into 25-year-old murdered in maximum security prison concludes
World.content:
Little could have been done to prevent an attack that led to the murder of a 25-year-old hours after he was moved to Auckland's maximum security prison, the prison's general manager says.

Blake Lee was shanked to death by another inmate in an exercise yard inside Auckland Prison at Paremoremo in March 2020.

A coronial inquest into his death at the Auckland District Court heard details about Lee's transfer to the prison hours before he was murdered.

Lee was killed in the prison yard soon after his transfer from Whanganui prison to Paremoremo.

The man responsible for his murder, Siuaki Lisiate, was a senior member of the Crips gang while Lee was an affiliate of the Mongrel Mob.

Auckland prison's current general manager Stephen Parr told the inquest's last day that he stood by his management of gangs inside the prison.

"I do mix gangs at Auckland prison," he said.

"In terms of the complexity, I would say we are pretty successful at it."

The inquest had earlier heard that at the time Lee was murdered, there was no set policy on where gang members should be placed in the prison.

Parr was asked by Coroner Alexander Ho about the difficulties of balancing a mix of different gang members in the prison yard, and about the potential of preventing what happened.

"Absent any overt indication to you that something was wrong, and I don't want to sound defeatist here, but there's little you can do to either foresee or prevent that?" Ho asked.

"That's correct sir, unfortunately, yes," Parr replied.

Yard numbers reduced

Parr had told the inquest on Thursday that current prison protocols would have prevented Lee from being placed into a mix on the day of his arrival.

The inquest heard from the principal corrections officer at the time, Gavin De Swardt, who said they had decreased the number of prisoners allowed to be in the yard, from seven or eight at a time to four.

At the time of Lee's murder, there were eight gang members in the yard, De Swardt said, including two members of the Mongrel Mob, two Crips, two Killer Beez and two others.

He was asked by Susan Gray, the lawyer representing Lee's mother, how much he knew about Lisiate's history of violence.

Lisiate had attacked double murderer Graeme Burton with a shank while both men were in Paremoremo, two years before Lee's murder.

"Is it fair to summarise that all you knew about Mr Lisiate was that he had a history of some serious violence?" Gray asked.

"That, and the day-to-day interactions with him, talking to him, and all that," De Swardt said.

Lisiate is one of 16 inmates in Auckland prison's Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit, the same unit housing the Christchurch terrorist.

Counsel assisting the Coroner, Martin Smith, asked De Swardt about mixing the gang members in the yard.

"It was just so we could even up the numbers," De Swardt said.

He was asked if bringing a new gang presence onto the prison wing could lead to tension.

"Sometimes it does, sometimes it has a calming effect," De Swardt said.

"I can give you examples of where we actually put Mongrel Mob with Mongrel Mob and they assault each other, it's like playing chess and trying to put a jigsaw puzzle together..."

De Swardt described Lee's murder as a spontaneous attack.

"It just came out of the blue," he said.

'Doesn't bring Blake back' - mother

Coroner Ho acknowledged Lee's mother, Teresa Absolum, who had been at the back of the courtroom since the beginning of the inquest.

"I would just like to express my condolences to you for Blake's death," he said.

"I'm sorry about the circumstances that have led you here. I hope that some of the matters we have discussed over the last two days has given you some answers, and that the burden that has been on you has lifted slightly."

Absolum told RNZ the inquest had answered some of her questions but "it doesn't bring Blake back".

She had earlier said it was painful to listen to the evidence as it brought up feelings of sadness and anger at the way her son died.

World.title: Government to retain Labour's clean car standard for imported high-emissions vehicles
World.content:
The government will retain a clean car standard that charges importers a fee for bringing high-emissions vehicles into the country.

However, it has not yet decided on the new limits that will be in force, saying it will work with the motor industry to develop settings that are "realistic and achievable".

Introduced by the previous government, the Clean Vehicle Standard charges importers a penalty for cars that exceed the target emissions level, but that can be offset by also importing cars with lower emissions.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop slashed the penalty by nearly 80 percent last November, saying supply constraints meant importers could not source enough low-emissions vehicles to avoid being penalised.

That could result in buyers paying thousands of dollars extra, Bishop said at the time.

Earlier this year, he launched a full review of the standard, which included an option to scrap it altogether.

That would have made New Zealand one of just two OECD countries to not have a vehicle emissions standard - the other is Russia.

Clean car advocates warned at the time that loosening the limits, or scrapping them altogether, would result in New Zealand being sold the high-emitting leftovers that manufacturers could no longer sell in Australia.

Australia introduced its own limits late last year, with the first six months of data showing overall tailpipe emissions had dropped and most importers were able to meet the standard.

Bishop said the decision to slash the standard last year was critical to ease pressure on importers and keep cars affordable.

However, the review had found the standard was "the most cost-effective way to increase the availability of lower-emissions vehicles in New Zealand", he said on Friday.

Most of the motor industry supported retaining some version of the standard, he said.

"In feedback on the review, industry noted that the standard is now well established in New Zealand, with importers accumulating credits and charges over time. Removing it at this stage would be highly disruptive for the vehicle industry."

The government would now go ahead with the next stage of the review, "to calibrate the settings so they are realistic and achievable for industry", Bishop said.

"The government has also agreed to set different targets for used vehicle imports to reflect that they have different and older technology."

Officials would report back early in 2027, and new targets and settings would take effect from 1 January, 2028.

A spokesperson for Bishop confirmed that the current settings would stay in place until then.

World.title: Teen's murder conviction and sentence to be reconsidered more than two decades on
World.content:
A teenager who murdered a truck driver with his own hammer will have her conviction and sentence reheard in court.

In 2003, Renee O'Brien was sentenced to life imprisonment for the 2002 murder of 60-year-old Waitara man Kenneth Pigott. She was just 14 at the time of the killing and was denied parole in 2014.

But Te Kāhui Tātari Ture / Criminal Cases Review Commission says it has obtained expert evidence that her "age, developmental stage and cognitive functioning may have affected her ability to understand and appreciate risk and form the intent required for murder".

"Te Kāhui also identified wider concerns affecting the fairness and reliability of the conviction," it said in a statement on Friday.

"This included O'Brien's ability to participate meaningfully in complex proceedings, uncertainty in the forensic pathology evidence, the late change of plea and evidence of a co-accused, party liability directions, and the use of O'Brien's police interview in her trial."

Acting deputy commissioner Professor Tracey McIntosh said their investigation posed "significant" questions.

"While no single issue necessarily determines the outcome, when considered together we concluded there were sufficient concerns for the Court of Appeal to consider her conviction again."

The commission also cited "significant developments in the law and understanding of adolescent neurological development and the sentencing of young people" since 2003, and that if sentenced today, it would be unlikely that she received a life sentence.

"Te Kāhui does not decide guilt or innocence, and a referral does not mean a conviction has been overturned," McIntosh said. "It means we have concluded that it is in the interests of justice for the case to be considered again by an appeal court."

O'Brien's lawyer Kerry Cook thanked Te Kāhui staff "for their diligent and thorough analysis of Renee’s case".

World.title: 'This is a united club': Swans AFLW captain and coach speak to media
World.content:
Sydney Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy has said her players have had "open conversations" in the wake of the scandal that has engulfed her club and led to five men's players being suspended for the rest of the season.

McEvoy, along with AFLW coach Colin O'Riordan, spoke to the media on Friday afternoon, saying the women's program supports the sanctions imposed on Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. The press conference has ended AFLW players would like to have say in whether five suspended men's players return Lucy McEvoy is asked if the AFLW players have discussed whether they want the five suspended players to return to the club. She tells the media that conversation has not happened but, when the time comes, the AFLW players would like to be part of the discussion. 'Moment for all women to stand together', McEvoy Here is more from Lucy McEvoy, speaking about the wider issue at the heart of this week's scandal. "There's no doubt, I think, a lot of women in the community are all feeling the same. "It's obviously an issue within the community that needs to be addressed, and I think this week it has been. "I applaud the club in the way they have handled it, and respected us as a women's program. "I think it's an important moment for all women to stand together and understand that all women deserve respect." Show more

Those five players will miss the remainder of the AFL season following club-imposed suspensions for breaking team standards in Melbourne earlier this week.

Victoria Police are investigating a sexual assault allegation, where it is alleged one player touched a woman without her consent. No charges have been laid, and no-one has been formally interviewed.

Speaking on Friday, McEvoy said the AFLW program supported the club-imposed suspensions to the five men's players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.

"On behalf of the playing group, we also support the club in the sanctions that were handed down," McEvoy said.

"To the players, we are incredibly disappointed, as a lot of people were.

"We know that the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club."

McEvoy said it had been a big week for the women's program, who will face Essendon at the Sydney Cricket Ground this weekend.

The Swans were hoping to celebrate this week's double-header with the men's round 24 clash with North Melbourne following the AFLW match on Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of this week's scandal, McEvoy said members of the women's program were processing their emotions and the situation.

"We've had some really open conversations as a group this week, and with the club more broadly," she said.

"We've felt the support both internally and externally as well.

"The girls are working through their emotions as they see fit for themselves."

When asked how this week has affected the reputation of the Sydney Swans, McEvoy said the club, both men's and women's teams, must work to regain the public's trust.

"There's no doubt the club has taken a reputational hit," she said.

"We will do whatever we can as a club, both programs, to make sure we build back the trust and respect of our members and fans, and the community more broadly."

O'Riordan, who played 34 AFL matches for the Swans between 2015 and 2022 before becoming the club's AFLW coach this season, said he was disappointed that he had to address this scandal.

"The actions of a small number of people have impacted a lot of people, especially the women in our football club and wider community," he said.

"As a man who was brought up with strong morals and a strong sense of what is right and wrong, [it's] disappointing to be standing here today and be talking about something like this.

"Growing up, I was always taught you treat everyone with respect, and that respect is a fundamental pillar of how you live your life.

"That is especially important in how you treat women."

O'Riordan said the club had remained "incredibly united" in the wake of the scandal.

"This is a united club. It always has been and always will be," he said.

World.title: Panthers NRL finals charge dealt blow by Cogger's three-match ban
World.content:
Penrith is in for a NRL finals selection dilemma after key addition Jack Cogger received a three-match ban for his high shot on Tyran Wishart.

Just when the streaky Panthers looked to have found their best option at five-eighth, Cogger received a grade-two charge that rules him out until after the first week of finals.

Unless Cogger can plead his case at the judiciary and win, the Panthers will be forced to recall out-of-favour Blaize Talagi or Perth-bound Jack Cole.

Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning The Penrith Panthers hold on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

Cogger was sent to the sin bin after rushing out of the line to hit Wishart late in the Panthers' 22-14 win on Thursday night.

He has already been suspended once this season for a similar shot, missing two weeks on that occasion for rushing out and hitting South Sydney's Ashton Ward.

If he unsuccessfully challenges his charge at the judiciary, Cogger will miss an additional game, potentially ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

Cogger also received a $3,000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash.

But the 29-year-old's suspension is a far bigger blow for a Penrith side fighting to lock up a top-two finish.

Cogger has been a valuable addition to the Panthers' starting side in recent weeks, proving a more assured defensive presence than Talagi.

His ball-playing has also helped take pressure off halfback Nathan Cleary, as it did during Penrith's comeback victory in the 2023 grand final.

But Cogger's illegal tackle has now opened the door for either Talagi or Cole, one of whom is set to start in the halves for next week's clash with Canterbury.

AAP

World.title: Swans captain 'deeply shocked' by scandal, denies player rift
World.content:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills have denied there is a rift in their playing group as they addressed the ongoing scandal engulfing the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

Dean Cox and Callum Mills addressed the media. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"As a playing group, we fully support the club's decisions on the sanctions handed down."

Mills said the five players would have to address the playing group, but there was no rift among the players.

Cox confirmed he was not in the room at the centre of the scandal, but would not say whether other staff members or players were present, as the club denied comments suggesting more men from the Swans were present in the room.

Both men refused to answer specific questions about what happened in the hotel room, saying they were the subject of a police investigation.

The Swans players and staff observed the press conference from behind the camera. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cox was also pressed on the club's decision to have the five suspended players driven back to Sydney from Melbourne, rather than flown.

"Decisions were made [as to] how we best support our players within the circumstances that happened," he said.

Cox admitted the club's previously acclaimed culture had "taken a hit".

"Our culture isn't perfect," he said.

"We're going to work as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been."

Live Moment Catch up up the key moments from Dean Cox and Callum Mills's press conference from Swans HQ. The press conference is over Dean Cox and Callum Mills have finished answering questions at Swans HQ. Cox's message to Sydney's fans ahead of the weekend Cox is asked what his message is to the club's fans considering coming to this weekend's games. "I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs. "We want to show that on Sunday." Is there concern for the mental health of the players? Mills is asked whether he is concerned for the mental health of the players suspended by the club. "There's concern in every part. That's the women in the community, our players involved, the women involved. "The wellbeing of everyone involved is [of] the utmost importance." Show more

Both Cox and Mills apologised to the club's AFLW team, with Mills saying he had addressed the group personally.

"I acknowledged their pain, and I deeply apologised for the actions of a few within our group," he said.

Cox added that he hoped the supporters would still come out in force for the double-header at the SCG this weekend.

"I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs," he said.

"We want to show that on Sunday."

Sydney's men's team rounds out its home and away season with a clash against North Melbourne on Sunday afternoon at the SCG, a match preceded by an AFLW match between Sydney's women's team and Essendon's women's team at the same venue.

World.title: 'Horrific consequences': Aussie star almost hit by car in Tour of Britain
World.content:
Australian cyclist Maeve Plouffe has revealed she nearly got hit by a car while riding in this week's Tour of Britain — and has warned of potentially more "horrific consequences" for a sport already reeling from tragedy.

Plouffe, the 27-year-old former Sydney track star who grabbed Commonwealth team pursuit gold and individual silver in 2022, prompted organisers of the week-long road race to review safety procedures after she outlined her "scary" experience.

Plouffe had to withdraw from the race, having suffered a puncture during the opening stage in Cumbria on Wednesday, and her revelation on Instagram about an alarming episode with a car as she attempted to chase back to the peloton.

Plouffe posted the statement of her close call on her personal Instagram account. (Instagram/@maeveplouffe)

Her comments came only days after British rider Finlay Tarling died last week during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal after he was hit by a non-race light goods vehicle that had entered the course.

Explaining her withdrawal, Plouffe added: "While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.

"Later on, the moto escort was wonderful, and I felt much safer.

"But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."

She was referring to the death of the 19-year-old Tarling, who was killed last week in a high-speed collision with a van, which had strayed onto the road during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

British rider Finlay Tarling (right) was killed by a non-race light goods vehicle during the Volta a Portugal last week. (Getty Images: Huw Fairclough)

Before the Tour of Britain Women had begun, an emotional tribute was paid to Tarling, with his picture projected onto a large screen while all 114 riders and roadside fans joined in a minute's applause to honour him.

Tarling was the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who will ride the Vuelta a España Grand Tour, which begins on Saturday, in honour of his sibling.

Organisers have swiftly taken note of Plouffe with Jonathan Day, events director of British Cycling Ventures — the commercial arm of British Cycling that organises the Tour — saying in a statement: "We're taking those comments extremely seriously."

"Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.

"We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.

"We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how seriously we are treating these comments."

The race continued on Thursday with Dutch superstar Lorena Wiebes claiming her second successive stage victory between Clitheroe and Blackpool but only after that second stage had been neutralised because of a car accident.

Australian rider Georgia Baker, fresh from her golden Commonwealth Games on the track in Glasgow, was also caught up in a crash on the route.

Wiebes is 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Chiara Consonni (Canyon-SRAM zondacrypto) in the general classification as the race moves into Wales on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Alcaraz confirms US Open return amid record prize money reveal
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz is set to return to action at the US Open, ending four months of injury torment, and will be back competing for a record grand slam winner's prize of $US5.5 million ($7.7 million) in New York.

The news of the seven-time grand slam winner's comeback at Flushing Meadows will be music to the ears of former Australian Open boss Craig Tiley, who has been able to begin his reign in charge of the US Open by announcing unprecedented riches to the players.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz has not played since April due to a concerning wrist injury.

He announced his return on Thursday in unusual fashion, with the help of football journalist Fabrizio Romano.

Romano, who is usually breaking news of big football transfers, used his catchphrase, "Here we go," to announce Alcaraz's return on Instagram, while the reigning champ repeated the message on X.

Alcaraz, who started the year by winning the Australian Open, has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in April. He has missed both the ‌French Open and ⁠Wimbledon while his great rival, Jannik Sinner, has largely dominated.

Now he is fit to return to the scene of his first grand slam triumph in 2022, when he became the youngest man to reach world number one in the rankings.

Alcaraz's return is fantastic news for Tiley, the former Tennis Australia CEO who has taken up the equivalent job at the US Tennis Association (USTA) and has been able to announce an overall prize fund of $US108 million — the first time the $US100m barrier has been broken at a slam.

Alcaraz's 2026 season has been cruelled by a wrist injury. (Getty Images: Quality Sport Images/Alvaro Medranda)

It is the biggest prize pot in the sport's history and represents a 20 per cent rise for the second consecutive year.

"This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners," Tiley said.

"We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players."

That platform is the formation of a Grand Slam Player Council, which is intended to give players a voice on a range of issues such as prize money.

Organisers hope all this will ward off the kind of player protests that occurred at the French Open and Wimbledon.

The champions' winning cheque will be $US5.5 million, up from the $5 million that Sabalenka and Alcaraz won last year.

Players will earn $US140,000 just for making it into the main draw, while a quarterfinalist earns $US780,000, a semifinalist $US1.45 million and runners-up $US2.8 million.

Meanwhile, there was good news for the Australian challenge following the withdrawal of Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina from the main draw through injury.

It meant Alexei Popyrin was able to be advanced to the main draw and the reciprocal wildcard he had been given by the USTA could instead go to his Australian teammate Dane Sweeny, who will make his Flushing Meadows debut at 25.

That takes the current Australian contingent set to start the action on August 30 to a total of 14 — eight men and six women — with more attempting to make it through next week's qualifying.

AAP

World.title: Test history looms, Renshaw returns as Australia and Bangladesh go again
World.content:
Australia was handed an historic, humbling nine-wicket defeat by Bangladesh in Darwin earlier this week.

It was the first time the Tigers had claimed a Test-match victory in Australia, and will have prompted some serious soul searching for the hosts, who were comprehensively second-best against the world's ninth ranked team.

Tomorrow morning, more history will be made, with Mackay's Harrup Park becoming the 12th Australian venue to host a Test when the teams begin the second and final match of the series.

You can listen to live coverage of the Test on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog

What needs to change for Mackay?: ABC Cricket Podcast

Australia has made one change to its squad for the encounter, with Matt Renshaw coming in for Jake Weatherald, while the return of an exciting young quick sees Bangladesh faced with a selection dilemma.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does the second Test begin?

The second Test between Australia and Bangladesh gets underway on Saturday August 22, with the first session of play beginning at 10am AEST in Mackay, QLD.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 9:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory (ACST), and 8am in Western Australia (AWST).

These are the session times for the five scheduled days of cricket:

First: 10:00am – 12:00pm AEST (9:30am — 11:30am ACST, 8:00am — 10:00am AWST)

10:00am – 12:00pm AEST (9:30am — 11:30am ACST, 8:00am — 10:00am AWST) Second: 12:40pm – 2:40pm AEST (12:10pm — 2:10pm ACST, 10:40am — 12:40pm AWST)

12:40pm – 2:40pm AEST (12:10pm — 2:10pm ACST, 10:40am — 12:40pm AWST) Third: 3:00pm – 5:00pm AEST (2:30pm — 4:30pm ACST, 1:00pm — 3:00pm AWST)
