Tech.content:
It’s back — or is it? After a seven-year absence, a ceramic case finish is reportedly returning to the Apple Watch lineup when the company launches its expected Series 12 lineup next month.

The tidbit comes from tech insider Kosutami, who posted on X, “Hell yeah, Ceramic Watch is back. We’ll see it at Series 12.” That backs up a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman earlier this month, which also said there would be a ceramic edition. Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.



If it happens, the ceramic finish will debut with several other products expected to launch at the next Apple event, which could take place as early as Sept. 9. Many analysts expect the company to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple’s first foldable phone.

Rare and expensive

Apple has only intermittently had watches with a ceramic finish. The first one, in white, came with the Series 2 watch line in 2016, followed by a gray option with Series 3 in 2017. After taking a year off, white ceramic returned in 2019 with the Series 5. There has been no ceramic option since.

The ceramic finishes were part of Apple’s Edition line, which also featured gold and titanium watches. Apple discontinued the Edition line after its final products in 2021.

The ceramic watches weren’t cheap. The debut in 2016 cost $1,249 for the 38mm version and $1,299 for the 42mm. In 2019, the ceramic model cost $1,299 for the 40mm and $1,349 for the 44mm.

When Apple unveiled its ceramic finish a decade ago, it said the casing was a combination of zirconia and alumina. A diamond slurry was used to mold each case for a “smooth surface and an exquisite shine.” Apple said the casing was four times harder than stainless steel, making it resistant to scratches and nicks.

Jon Rettinger, a tech influencer with over 1.66 million YouTube subscribers, says the ceramic model has been his favorite version of the Apple Watch.



“While absurdly expensive, its unique look won a spot on my wrist,” Rettinger told CNET. “Every fall when they announce a new gen, a small part of me hopes ceramic comes back.”

Apple is the market leader in smartwatches, according to research firm Counterpoint. Apple accounted for 23% of all global shipments in the first quarter of the year, followed by Huawei at 17%. Apple also had a 21% growth in shipments from the previous year.

Tech.title: Stressed Parents Mean More Screen Time for Kids, Study Finds. That’s Trouble for Back-to-School Season
Tech.content:
As a parent, I know how easy it is to use screen time as a way to keep my kid busy — whether it’s TV, learning apps or FaceTime with family, it may buy me a few minutes.

I’m not alone: A new study from Florida International University’s Center for Children and Families finds that stressed parents are more likely to turn to their screens and devices to keep their kids busy or calm. And those parents are less likely to enforce screen-time limits.

That may have been OK for summer break. However, many kids are already back in school. And the early mornings and class time can be a tough transition for families — especially for kids who are used to more time on their tablets. So what should parents do?

Screen time is determined by parents’ stress

FIU’s study evaluated 822 caregivers of children ages 4 to 8 through online surveys on the child’s behaviors, parenting stress and screen-time strategies. The findings show that parents opt for more screen time when a child’s behavior seems difficult and how much time is usually less enforced.

Shayl Griffith, an assistant professor in FIU’s Department of Counseling, Recreation and School Psychology and the senior author of the study, said in a statement that parents shouldn’t be afraid to ask for help. The study’s recommendation is to focus on screen time and media that are “meaningful, engaging and appropriate for their child’s age.”

“When caregivers have the resources they need, they are better able to set consistent boundaries and engage with their children in ways that promote healthy development,” Griffith said.

The fine line between digital media discipline and disruption

Youth screen time is a growing concern. In January, the American Academy of Pediatrics published findings on correlations between digital media use and age-related development to help determine screen time rules for your child and monitor behavior.

Toddlers and kindergarteners who use digital media for high-quality educational content can benefit from good social behaviors and language — especially when a caregiver is viewing the screen and interacting with the child. However, young children who use tablets for hours, but the AAP says too much screen time is linked to angry outbursts.

Children ages 6 to 12 can benefit from thoughtful educational digital media in moderation, the AAP study found. But again, there are risks. Too much media use can lead to lower academic achievement, attention control and cognition. Some media can be problematic for kids, like apps encouraging purchases, those focused on gaming with not much educational value, and content that is dangerous or risky. And there’s a big callout included in the list: school devices that give access to “distracting video games, videos and other platforms.”

Managing stress, school and screen time is tricky

With summer wrapping up and school approaching, the big question is: How should stressed parents think about screen time? School may be the solution.

“School can help provide a reprieve for families who do not have access to childcare in the summertime months and serve as a helpful jumping-off point to re-evaluate digital media habits, given the change in routine already,” said Dr. Tiffany Munzer, a professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School. It can also mean more time for in-person interactions, which is important for social connection, Munzer added.

Jeff Temple, a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, who was not affiliated with the FIU study, said screen time to get through the day is mostly OK during summer break, but that can make the back-to-school season a challenge for kids, Temple said. Adjusting screen time while managing life stresses may not be easy.

Munzer recommends making incremental changes. For example, if your child loves watching do-it-yourself videos, find a way to recreate what they’re seeing, Munzer said. Or if digital media is a way to calm kids, look for alternative activities such as reading or walking, Munzer added.

Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco, said the back-to-school season is a good time to revisit family screen time rules and routines.

“Rather than simply trying to return to an old set of rules, families can consider what makes sense for the child’s current age, developmental stage, school schedule and use of devices for schoolwork and communication,” said Nagata. “A family media plan should be dynamic; it may reasonably look different during the school year than during summer or holidays, and on weekdays compared with weekends.”

The AAP recommends creating a Family Media Plan based on your family’s needs. The plan is an agreement that lets you prioritize healthy, safe and consistent screen time boundaries. That includes creating a list of approved media kids can choose from, a schedule of screen-free time, how to choose good media content and outlets for your family.

Experts also recommend the AAP’s 5 C’s of Media Use, tailored to your child’s age. The five C’s are Child, Content, Calm, Crowding Out and Communication. They can help you set and communicate screen time guidelines based on your child, their emotions, the content and how it affects them. That may not help the stress that parents face, but it could help regulate your child’s screen time without guilt.

Nagata encourages parents to pay attention to their children’s time and relationship with screen time. Look out for warning signs like difficulty cutting back on screen time despite trying, becoming preoccupied with social media or a phone, experiencing conflict because of screen use and using screens to escape problems. And pay attention to see if screen use is interfering with sleep, school relationships or other activities so you can make more adjustments sooner.

Tech.title: Where Vandals Can’t Reach? Flock Safety’s Future Is Full of Spying Drones
Tech.content:
Surveillance company Flock Safety, one of the most controversial technology companies in the US, is expanding its footprint beyond automated license plate readers and its vast AI-powered camera network. Facing growing backlash over its partnership with law enforcement and its tracking of activists and protesters, Flock is now betting on drones — flying cameras dispatched from the sky for use in first-responder situations.

Civil liberties groups and digital rights advocates have long warned that Flock’s surveillance network, which relies on the broad collection and sharing of location data, poses a threat to individual privacy. If anything, the recent publicity over its burgeoning drone business will only intensify scrutiny of a vendor already under fire.

During an appearance on the All-In Podcast, Flock CEO and founder Garrett Langley gave the clearest indication yet of how much of a role drones will play in Flock’s future.

Describing drones as the company’s “fastest-growing business unit right now,” Langley said on the podcast that drones will account for nearly half of the company’s future revenue. He described drones as “the next big chapter in law enforcement,” with the potential to be as impactful as police body cameras.

Reading license plates from the sky

The emphasis on drones comes with the spread of “deflock” actions and grassroots opposition to license plate readers. After complaints that the LPRs can misidentify vehicles and that Flock’s network can be abused to target vulnerable populations, cities, including Los Angeles, have paused or canceled their contracts with the company.

In some communities, activists have taken down Flock cameras or physically disabled the hardware as a form of protest against surveillance. Organizations and individuals have crowdsourced the locations of local cameras, while municipalities that asked Flock to disable the cameras have put trash bags on them when their requests weren’t met.

Drones equipped with high-resolution cameras could be even more capable of identifying license plate numbers and tracking vehicle movement. And, of course, they’re harder to disable from the ground.

Instead of responding to a request for comment, the company sent CNET an automated response via email that read in part: “Our media team is currently touching grass and taking a break. Unlike our cameras, we can’t work 24/7, so we’ll get back to you when we’ve had a snack and regained the ability to form coherent sentences.”

Safety versus privacy

Flock’s website has product pages for drones that can be used as first-responder units in emergencies or by companies as automated security devices. The company told Business Insider that it plans to start manufacturing its own drones in Georgia and has about 200 of them deployed as first-responder devices.

During the All-In Podcast interview, Langley acknowledged that Flock sits dead center in the debate over personal privacy versus community safety. “What kind of society do we want to live in? I want to live in one where we’re safer. I want to keep my privacy while I do it, but it’s hard,” he said. “We’ve gotta find a common ground.”

Langley said that, unlike some of Flock’s competitors, the company does not use its cameras (presumably including those on drones) for facial recognition or for looking inside cars.

However, a recent investigation from Wired found that the company already has code that would expand its product’s capabilities to identify drivers and vehicles based on their movement patterns alone. While Flock Safety maintains that the software remains in a testing phase, privacy critics argue that the tool — called OS Investigate — integrates vehicle scan data with police incident reports and arrest records, transforming Flock’s camera network into a powerful system for generating suspect lists.

The expanded capabilities of drones used for surveillance have been met with criticism from the American Civil Liberties Union, which issued a report in March about the privacy dangers they present.

“If there is a drone in the sky above us, we should have a way to know whether that drone belongs to Amazon, the police, ICE, a real estate agent, or an ordinary citizen,” the ACLU report said. “We should also be able to see what the purpose of its flight is, what equipment it is carrying, and what its privacy practices are.”

Tech.title: Marley Spoon, Blue Apron Face Delivery Issues After Food Supplier Bankruptcy
Tech.content:
I tested Marley Spoon for the first time last year. I loved the prompt shipment, creative dishes and fresh ingredients. Overall, it was one of the most impressive meal kit brands I’ve ever tried. That’s why the box I received this week seemed so jarring.

To start, my most recent Marley Spoon box was delivered on Tuesday instead of its scheduled delivery date of Monday. It was also missing multiple ingredients along with every market item I ordered. The produce was comically small, and a melted ice pack made everything wet and soggy. I’ve tried dozens of meal kits over the past two years, but this type of disappointment was a first.

It appears that, compared to others, I got off relatively easy. Many customers, sharing their grievances on Marley Spoon’s Instagram page, have missed upward of 75% of their ingredients or received entirely incorrect orders.

In a statement to CNET, a spokesperson for Marley Spoon said the issues are tied to an “operational transition.”

“We take this very seriously and are working around the clock to ensure our customers receive their boxes on time, with the correct, high-quality ingredients they expect from Marley Spoon,” the statement said. “We expect these issues to improve as we progress with the transition, and we’ll keep our customers updated along the way.”

My pecan-crusted salmon with sweet potato fries was missing five ingredients. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

What’s causing the issues with food delivery boxes?

Earlier this year, FreshRealm, a major US food supplier that acquired Marley Spoon’s US fulfillment operations in 2024, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The filing came nearly a year after a large recall of ready-to-eat chicken alfredo meals supplied by FreshRealm occurred due to possible listeria contamination.

The size of this sweet potato, meant to be a side portion for two people, was possibly the most shocking item in my box. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

The disruptions have also hit Blue Apron, another meal kit front-runner, with the company providing a similar statement to CNET, stating that the issues arose during a “transition to a new fulfillment partner.”

“We haven’t delivered the reliability our customers count on — so for now, we’re temporarily focusing our menu on what we’re confident we can deliver, adding quality checks before boxes ship, and making progress with our partners to fix what’s broken,” the statement said. “We appreciate our customers’ patience and hope to regain their trust by delivering the experience they signed up for.”

After Blue Apron released a statement on Instagram, customers echoed complaints seen among Marley Spoon customers, with some claiming they received spoiled boxes or no box at all. They also state difficulty getting in contact with the company.

In April of this year, CNET reported that Blue Apron was expected to transition to working with Misfits Market as its new food distributor after FreshRealm’s bankruptcy filing.

Ken Shuman, a Misfits Market spokesperson, confirmed to CNET that the company also began fulfilling Marley Spoon’s orders the last week of July.

“Our operations and fulfillment role for Marley Spoon is the same as our role with Blue Apron,” Shuman said in an email.

When will the supply chain issues be resolved?

Neither Marley Spoon nor Blue Apron answered additional questions regarding the current issues, and neither company provided a timeline for when the supply chain issues are expected to be fixed. However, Shuman provided some context regarding the transition, stating that the company has “compressed what’s typically a 10 [to] 12 month transition into under 10 weeks.”

In addition to taking over order fulfillment, Shuman stated that the company is also handling inventory management, onboarding hundreds of employees and “taking on fulfillment across our facilities nationwide.”

“An operational transition at that speed has real challenges, and the biggest one has been inventory,” Shuman added. “Some gaps were more significant than we initially understood, and we’ve been working through them with Blue Apron and with vendors every step of the way. We’re starting to see meaningful improvement and expect that to continue.”

When items were missing from my Marley Spoon order, I was credited $45.23 to my next order, rather than refunded to the credit card I used. This credit came from missing these items in my box: Margherita Pizza and Famous Original Pizza (both market items), parmesan, panko, dill, mint and mayonnaise.

But a credit means the only way to recoup the money is to give Marley Spoon another shot. I’m willing to do that, considering I’ve loved the service in the past. But the question remains, what if the next order is missing items, too? Are customers expected to keep ordering boxes to get back the money they’ve already spent?

I asked both Marley Spoon customer service and a spokesperson what a customer should do if they want a refund rather than a credit, but did not hear back in time for publication. CNET has also reached out to FreshRealm for comment.

Have you experienced delivery or ingredient issues from any meal delivery kit companies? Let us know. Email me at ccesaric@cnet.com.
